div.head: II
div.p: The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore

div.head: IV
div.p: The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore important information for explaining population growth rates. Brown bears (Ursus arctos) are large-bodied hibernators that gestate, give birth, and begin lactating in the den during hibernation while consuming no additional foods or water. Thus, females undergo the most energetically taxing event in mammalian life history during a long fast and under extreme metabolic circumstances. Even though brown bears belong to the order Carnivora, many populations consume little meat, relying on vegetation, hard and soft mast, and invertebrates.

The diverse brown bear diet suggests that they are highly adaptable to local conditions, which makes them an ideal species to study changes in climate and phenology, because we expect them to rapidly alter their behavior and foraging. Here, we determine how life history is affected by diet and physiological demands and how diet changes annually in response to resource availability. We used stable isotope and cortisol data as indices of diet and metabolic demands in addition to individual body condition indices and reproductive output from an individually marked brown bear population in southcentral Sweden. To address the larger research topic, this thesis focused on five specific research questions:1) do diet estimates from stable isotopes match previous estimates from scat analysis and ecological theory; 2) how does age and reproductive state affect cortisol concentrations in this population of brown bears; 3) how does resource availability and metabolic demands affect the life history trade-off between growth and reproduction; 4) are Scandinavian brown bears smaller than North American brown bears and what determines variation in growth; 5) how does brown bear diet change with annual variation in resource availability. We used Bayesian mixing models in R to estimate dietary proportions of the five main foods in our system (ants; Formica and Camponotus spp., bilberry; Vaccinium myrtillius, crowberry; Empetrum nigrum, lingonberry; Vaccinium vitis-idaea, and moose; Alces alces) and published data to estimate the proportion of fats, lipids, and carbohydrates, and energy content of brown bear diet. We used linear regression modelling to explain variance in cortisol, growth and body sizes, female reproductive investments, and trends in brown bear diet over time. We built models based on a priori hypotheses and used and information-V The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore theoretic framework to compare models. When we evaluated the individual model components, we used the extent to which the confidence or credible intervals overlapped zero as well as the amount of variation in the data explained by the model in question when compared to a similar model (i.e., differing by a single model component). Confidence or credible intervals with no overlap = strong evidence, some overlap (< ~10%) = moderate evidence, and intervals that overlapped zero by > 15% was weak evidence for a relationship between the covariate and the response variable in the equation. Brown diet estimated using stable isotopes did not resemble estimates from previous scat analyses and most closely resembled predictions from the optimum foraging theory, although none of the models fully described the relationship between brown bear foraging and community interactions in our system (question 1). The % dry matter proportions and metabolizable energy provided by proteins in Scandinavian brown bear diet was much lower than predicted-Scandinavian bears primarily consumed bilberries and lingonberries, followed by crowberries, ants, and moose. Cortisol concentrations measured in brown bear hair varied among demographic classes, as well as with age (question 2). Solitary bears had the lowest cortisol concentrations and females with dependent offspring had substantially higher concentrations, while dependent offspring had the highest concentrations. Cortisol is predominately a metabolic steroid hormone and reflects the energetic demands of organisms, therefore, higher cortisol concentrations are likely related to the extraordinary metabolic demands that developing offspring and reproducing females' experience. Offspring mass was greater with heavier mothers and lower in larger litters and in years with higher bear density (question 3). Variation in the mass difference between mothers and offspring was best explained by the model that accounted for the effects of residual maternal mass, maternal δ 15 N, litter size, and bear density. This suggests that when energetic demands increase beyond some unknown threshold, females pass the burden onto their offspring.

Brown bear size was different between North America and Scandinavia, but only for females (question 4). Alberta females were heavier and longer than Swedish females and there was VI The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore a positive effect of NDVI on female size. The capture model was the most parsimonious model to explain variation in male mass between the study areas and contained no habitat variables. Through time, there is evidence that the proportion of ants and moose in the diet have decreased, whereas the proportion of bilberry in the diet has remained stable or slightly increased (question 5). Variation in δ 13 C values was negatively correlated with bilberry productivity and the number of moose calves observed in the year in which hair was grown.

Variation in δ 15 N values was best described by the model that accounted for the effects of bear age, sex, an interaction between age and sex, and bilberry production the year prior to hair growth. Brown bear diet in Scandinavia seems to be driven directly by primary productivity, with bears either consuming more higher-trophic foods or catabolizing their own tissues to meet energetic requirements following years with poor bilberry production, which is surprising for an "apex predator". These results highlight the importance of expanding our views of species and ecological principals beyond narrow human constructs, such as "carnivore" and "apex predator". Human constructs around nature that become too narrow lead to comparisons which can minimize the views and novel research questions. No single population or life history is superior to others. Instead, each iteration is a unique result from different selection pressures. Rather than focusing on what makes one population "more fit" than the other, ecologists should focus on the environmental limitations that drive differences among individuals, populations, or species and the unique adaptations that arise due to environmental limitations. Understanding the diverse adaptations required to meet metabolic demands under extreme conditions and the evolutionary processes that shape and maintain these adaptations is critical to conserving ecosystem processes. This research project has expanded our understanding of both brown bear ecology as well as the larger ecological theories within our discipline. Yet these are only a foundation on which to build a better understanding of life-history trade-offs in the face of extreme metabolic demands, such as giving birth and lactation during a long fast.

div.head: VII
div.p: The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Norsk Mange økologiske prinsipper er bygget på relasjoner som forbinder en organismes kosthold, plassbruk og kondisjon. Imidlertid er det komplisert å aktualisere disse teoretiske forholdene til virkelighet, fordi en organismes kondisjon er et resultat av mange komplekse interaksjoner.
Når det gjelder kosthold, for eksempel, er polyfagi utbredt i ordenen Carnivora, men det er en tendens til å fokusere kun på animalsk avledet mat når man vurderer kostholdskvalitet.

Dermed skaper en overforenklet rolle for rovdyr i økologiske samfunn som utelukker mange trofiske interaksjoner som kan vaere viktige for samfunnsstabilitet, spesielt gitt menneskeskapte endringer i miljøet eller endringer på grunn av klimaendringer. Endringer i primaerproduktivitet og andre samfunnsinteraksjoner kan føre til endringer i artenes livshistorie når de tilpasser seg endringer i ressurstilgjengelighet mediert gjennom avveininger mellom matkvalitet og tilgjengelighet. Økologisk teori forutsier at organismer vil tilpasse sin fôringsatferd og energiallokering mellom vekst og reproduksjon på en bestemt måte, basert på deres livshistorier. Det er imidlertid variasjon mellom populasjoner og individer innen arter som avviker fra forventningene, men som er lokalt tilpasningsdyktige, for eksempel mødre som endrer energiinvesteringen sin i reproduksjon. Avkom av mødre som investerer mer ressurser i reproduksjon har en tendens til å ha høyere livstidskondisjon enn avkom av mødre som investerer faerre ressurser. Derfor kan lokale tilpasninger til landskapsendringer som endrer mors investeringer påvirke populasjonskondisjonsmålinger.

Større investering i hvert reproduksjonsforsøk kan resultere i hunner som vokser saktere eller når en mindre asymptotisk kroppsstørrelse, noe som kan redusere livslang reproduksjonsproduksjon og overlevelse. Samlet sett kan fôrmønstre, så vel som ressursanskaffelse og allokering påvirke befolkningsvekst og stabilitet gjennom reproduktiv produksjon og kvinnelig overlevelse. Å forstå sammenhengene mellom miljø, vekst, kroppsstørrelsesmålinger og reproduktive investeringer gir derfor viktig informasjon for å VIII The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore forklare befolkningsvekstrater. Brunbjørn (Ursus arctos) er store dvaleviner som blir gravide, føder og begynner å amme i hiet under dvalemodus mens de ikke inntar ekstra mat eller vann. Dermed gjennomgår hunner den mest energisk belastende hendelsen i pattedyrs livshistorie under en lang faste og under ekstreme metabolske omstendigheter. Selv om brunbjørn tilhører ordenen Carnivora, spiser mange populasjoner lite kjøtt, avhengig av vegetasjon, hard og myk mast og virvelløse dyr. Den mangfoldige brunbjørndietten antyder at de er svaert tilpasningsdyktige til lokale forhold, noe som gjør dem til en ideell art for å studere endringer i klima og fenologi, fordi vi forventer at de raskt endrer atferd og fôr. Her bestemmer vi hvordan livshistorien påvirkes av kosthold og fysiologiske krav og hvordan kostholdet endres årlig som svar på ressurstilgjengelighet. Vi brukte stabile isotop-og kortisoldata som indekser for kosthold og metabolske behov i tillegg til individuelle kroppstilstandsindekser og reproduksjonsproduksjon fra en individuelt merket brunbjørnbestand i Sør-Midt-Sverige. For å adressere det større forskningstemaet, fokuserte denne avhandlingen på fem spesifikke forskningsspørsmål: 1) samsvarer diettestimater fra stabile isotoper med tidligere estimater fra scat-analyse og økologisk teori; 2) hvordan påvirker alder og reproduksjonstilstand kortisolkonsentrasjonen i denne populasjonen av brunbjørner; 3) hvordan påvirker ressurstilgjengelighet og metabolske krav livshistorieavveiningen mellom vekst og reproduksjon; 4) er skandinavisk brunbjørn mindre enn nordamerikansk brunbjørn og det som bestemmer variasjon i vekst; 5) Hvordan endres brunbjørnens diett med årlig variasjon i ressurstilgjengelighet. Vi brukte Bayesianske blandingsmodeller i R for å estimere kostholdsandeler av de fem viktigste matvarene i systemet vårt (maur; Formnica og Camponotus spp., blåbaer; Vaccinium myrtillius, kråkebaer; Empetrum nigrum, tyttebaer; Vaccinium vitis-idaea og elg; Alces alces) og publiserte data for å estimere andelen fett, lipider og karbohydrater, og energiinnholdet i brunbjørndietten. Vi brukte lineaer regresjonsmodellering for å forklare varians i kortisol, vekst og kroppsstørrelser, kvinnelige reproduktive investeringer og trender i brunbjørndiett over tid. Vi bygde modeller basert på a priori hypoteser og brukte et informasjonsteoretisk rammeverk

div.head: IX
div.p: The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore for å sammenligne modeller. Da vi evaluerte de enkelte modellkomponentene, brukte vi i hvilken grad konfidensintervallene eller troverdige intervaller overlappet null, samt mengden variasjon i dataene som ble forklart av den aktuelle modellen sammenlignet med en lignende modell (dvs. differensierende med en enkelt modellkomponent). Konfidens eller troverdige intervaller uten overlapping = sterk evidens, noe overlapping (< ~10 %) = moderat evidens, og intervaller som overlappet null med > 15 % var svake bevis for en sammenheng mellom kovariaten og responsvariabelen i ligningen. Brun diett estimert ved hjelp av stabile isotoper lignet ikke estimater fra tidligere scat-analyser og lignet mest på prediksjoner fra teorien om optimal fôring, selv om ingen av modellene fullt ut beskrev forholdet mellom brunbjørnens fôring og samfunnsinteraksjoner i systemet vårt (spørsmål 1). % tørrstoffandeler og metaboliserbar energi levert av proteiner i skandinavisk brunbjørndiett var mye lavere enn spådd -skandinaviske bjørner spiste først og fremst blåbaer og tyttebaer, etterfulgt av kråkebaer, maur og elg. Kortisolkonsentrasjoner målt i brunbjørnehår varierte mellom demografiske klasser, så vel som med alder (spørsmål 2). Solitaere bjørner hadde de laveste kortisolkonsentrasjonene og hunner med avkom hadde vesentlig høyere konsentrasjoner, mens avhengige avkom hadde de høyeste konsentrasjonene. Kortisol er hovedsakelig et metabolsk steroidhormon og gjenspeiler de energiske kravene til organismer, derfor er høyere kortisolkonsentrasjoner sannsynligvis relatert til de ekstraordinaere metabolske kravene som utvikler avkom og reproduserer kvinners opplevelse. Avkomsmassen var større hos tyngre mødre og lavere i større kull og i år med høyere bjørnetetthet (spørsmål 3).
Variasjon i masseforskjellen mellom mødre og avkom ble best forklart av modellen som tok hensyn til effekten av gjenvaerende mormasse, mors δ15N, kullstørrelse og bjørnetetthet.

Dette antyder at når energikravene øker utover en ukjent terskel, overfører hunnene byrden til avkommet. Brunbjørnstørrelsen var forskjellig mellom Nord-Amerika og Skandinavia, men bare for hunner (spørsmål 4). Alberta-hunner var tyngre og lengre enn svenske hunner, og det var en positiv effekt av NDVI på hunnstørrelsen. Fangstmodellen var den mest sparsommelige modellen for å forklare variasjon i mannlig masse mellom studieområdene og X The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore inneholdt ingen habitatvariabler. Over tid er det dokumentert at andelen maur og elg i kostholdet har gått ned, mens andelen blåbaer i kosten har holdt seg stabil eller litt økt (spørsmål 5). Variasjon i δ13C-verdier var negativt korrelert med blåbaerproduktivitet og antall elgkalver observert i året håret ble dyrket. Variasjon i δ15N-verdier ble best beskrevet av modellen som tok hensyn til effekten av bjørnealder, kjønn, et samspill mellom alder og kjønn, og blåbaerproduksjon året før hårvekst. Brunbjørndiett i Skandinavia ser ut til å vaere drevet direkte av primaerproduktivitet, med bjørner som enten spiser mer høytrofisk mat eller kataboliserer sitt eget vev for å møte energibehov etter år med dårlig blåbaerproduksjon, noe som er overraskende for et "apex-rovdyr". Disse resultatene fremhever viktigheten av å utvide vårt syn på arter og økologiske prinsipper utover smale menneskelige konstruksjoner, som "kjøtteter" og "apex-rovdyr". Menneskelige konstruksjoner rundt naturen som blir for snevre fører til sammenligninger som kan minimere synspunktene og nye forskningsspørsmål. Ingen enkelt befolkning eller livshistorie er overlegen andre. I stedet er hver iterasjon et unikt resultat fra forskjellige seleksjonstrykk. I stedet for å fokusere på hva som gjør den ene populasjonen "mer egnet" enn den andre, bør økologer fokusere på miljøbegrensningene som driver forskjeller mellom individer, populasjoner eller arter og de unike tilpasningene som oppstår på grunn av miljøbegrensninger. Å forstå de ulike tilpasningene som kreves for å møte metabolske krav under ekstreme forhold og de evolusjonaere prosessene som former og opprettholder disse tilpasningene er avgjørende for å bevare økosystemprosesser. Dette forskningsprosjektet har utvidet vår forståelse av både brunbjørnøkologi så vel som de større økologiske teoriene innen vår disiplin. Likevel er disse bare et grunnlag for å bygge en bedre forståelse av livshistorieavveininger i møte med ekstreme metabolske krav, som fødsel og amming under en lang faste. div.head: Theoretical background
div.p: Many ecological principles are built on theoretical relationships connecting an organism's diet, where they exist within their ecosystem, and their fitness (Darwin, 1839;MacArthur & Pianka 1966). However, actualizing these theoretical relationships is complicated, because an organism's fitness is the result of many complex interactions, both physiological and environmental, which often vary among individuals and populations (Laughlin & Messier, 2015;Walter et al., 2018). For carnivores, our understanding of diet, community interactions, and fitness is skewed towards charismatic "apex predators", in which prey availability is the primary driver for explaining fitness (Hatton et al., 2015;Jonzén et al., 2013). Despite the prevalence of polyphagy (also referred to as omnivory) within the order Carnivora (Gittleman, 2013), there is a tendency to focus on animal-derived foods when assessing diet quality (Alkerwi, 2014;McLellan, 2011;Steyaert et al., 2012). Protein acquisition is often considered the highest priority for foraging choices (Erlenbach et al., 2014;Kohl et al., 2015;Robbins et al., 2007, but see Robbins et al., 2022 andRothman et al., 2011), with other diet components arising from either a scarcity of prey or as a strategy to over-eat low-protein foods (Erlenbach et al., 2014;Felicetti et al., 2003;Simpson & Raubenheimer, 2005). Thus, the historical focus on interactions between large, obligate carnivores and their prey oversimplifies the roles of carnivores within ecological communities (Kohl et al., 2015;Miller et al., 2001) and excludes numerous trophic interactions that may be important to community stability (Cruz-McDonnell & Wolf, 2016;Garay et al., 2012;Hunter, 2009;Kratina et al., 2012), particularly given anthropogenic alterations to the environment (Gutgesell et al., 2022).

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore resource allocation to offspring during egg production (Li et al., 2022) or gestation and lactation (Gutierrez- Marcos et al., 2012;Robbins et al., 2012). Offspring of mothers which invest more resources in reproduction tend to have higher lifetime fitness than offspring of mothers which invest fewer resources (Van de Pol et al., 2006). Therefore, local adaptations that result in females investing more or fewer resources in their offspring can affect offspring survival, recruitment, and within-population trends (Rollinson & Rowe, 2016) or amongpopulation differences (Taillon et al., 2013) in fitness metrics. Female phenotypes which invest more in reproduction than self-maintenance and growth may also result in females that grow slower or reach a smaller asymptotic body size. Body size is an important life history trait that is positively associated with both reproduction and survival (Robbins et al., 2012;Stearns, 1989), and is a product of both natural selection (Arnold & Wade, 1984;Stearns, 1989) and human-caused selection (Coltman et al., 2003;Darimont et al., 2009). Typically, individuals or populations that exhibit relatively small body sizes are assumed to be the result of stunted growth related to nutritional limitations (Baldwin & Sains, 1995). Comparing populations is one way to determine drivers of body size variation and fitness costs.

Collectively, foraging patterns, as well as resource acquisition, and allocation can affect population growth and stability through reproductive output and female survival (Saether et al., 2013). Thus, understanding the links between the environment, growth, body size metrics, and reproductive investments provides important information for explaining population growth rates.

div.head: Physiological indices
div.p: However, life history traits, such as resource acquisition through diet, are difficult to measure.

Methods to estimate diet have evolved from observational studies and gut content analysis to more nuanced methods, such as stable isotope analysis. Stable isotope analysis is based on the principal that all tissues within an organism must be made from components of its

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore environment, whether that is soil and water for autotrophs or food components in the case of heterotrophs (Gannes et al., 1998). Thus, stable isotope analysis not only indicates what an animal has eaten, but also how that animal assimilates foods into its body (Cherel et al., 2005;Tieszen & Boutton, 1989). Differences in environment and physiology result in naturally varying isotopic signatures, and in the case of consumers, an individual's stable isotope composition will be more similar to the most dominant component of its diet (Gannes et al., 1998).

In addition to understanding the energy and nutritional content of an organism's diet, it is also important to understand the overall metabolic demands or physiological state of that organism. In this way, we include the energetic income, as well as the energetic expenses, to explain differences among populations or individuals (van Noordwijk & de Jong, 1986).

Certain steroid hormones, particularly corticosterone and cortisol, are useful energetic indicators, due to their roles in both predictable day-to-day metabolic functions, as well as their role in the vertebrate stress response (Landys et al., 2006;Sapolsky, 2000). At baseline levels, these hormones serve predominantly metabolic functions, but as demand for energy increases, the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis increases concentrations, which activates alternate physiological pathways, commonly referred to as the vertebrate stress response (Landys et al., 2006). Because keratinized structures (such as hair and nails) develop relatively slowly, cortisol concentrations from these tissues are long-term indicators of an animal's physiological state (Cattet et al., 2018;Koren et al., 2019). Coupled with indicators of body condition and diet, cortisol can give important context to energy allocation in wild animals (Fairhurst et al., 2015;Schillaci et al., 2019).

div.head: Study species and research questions
div.p: The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Evolution has resulted in animals with a variety of strategies to deal with resource limitations.

For example, many species use torpor or hibernation as a strategy to reduce their metabolic rate, and their energy requirements, during periods of low food availability (Scopes et al., 2024). Brown bears (Ursus arctos) are large-bodied hibernators that mate early in the active season and then maximize foraging to store enough energy and nutrients to sustain them through hibernation (Craighead & Mitchell, 1982). Female brown bears gestate, give birth, and begin lactating in the den during hibernation while consuming no additional foods or water (Friebe et al., 2014;López-Alfaro et al., 2013). Thus, female brown bears undergo the most energetically taxing event in mammalian life history during a long fast and under extreme metabolic circumstances. Further, during denning, reproducing females are in a semi closed system in which resources are transmitted directly from mother to offspring with little external input (Lopez-Alfaro et al., 2013). Therefore, this species represents an interesting model for understanding how organisms obtain and allocate resources. Brown bears have a large, circumpolar distribution and use a variety of landscapes and foods (Bojarska & Selva, 2012;Diserens et al., 2020). Their wide geographic distribution means that generalizations may be applicable across different parts of the world (Zedrosser et al., 2011) and that comparing populations in different areas of their range may highlight important evolutionary or landscape differences (Ferguson & McLaughlin, 2000;Hildebrand et al., 2019;Swenson et al., 2007). Their diverse diet suggests that they are highly adaptable to local conditions, which makes them an ideal species to study changes in climate and phenology, because we expect them to rapidly alter their behavior and foraging (Bojarska & Selva, 2012;Deacy et al., 2017). Even though brown bears belong to the order Carnivora, many populations consume little meat; relying on vegetation, hard and soft mast, and invertebrates (Bojarska & Selva, 2012;Diserens et al., 2020). However, meat is the most efficiently digested food in brown bear diets (Pritchard & Robbins, 1990), and greater carnivory in brown bears is positively associated with population density, body size, and reproductive output (Hilderbrand et al., 1999;Mowat & Heard, 2006;Zedrosser et al., 2006), partially due to greater fixed nitrogen and energy density at higher trophic levels (Elser et al., 2000). Thus, there is a direct connection between brown bear diet, physiology, and fitness.
The broad intention of this research was to determine how life history is affected by diet and physiological demands and how diet changes annually in response to resource availability
We used data from an individually-marked brown bear population in southcentral Sweden that has been monitored by the Scandinavian Brown Bear Research Project for 40 years.
Data included individual reproductive information, stable isotope values, and cortisol concentrations measured in hair across the population, including mothers and their yearling offspring.
To address the larger research topic, this thesis focused on five specific research questions:

div.head: Study system
div.p: The study area is ~20,000 km2 located in Gävleborg and Dalarna counties, southcentral Sweden. Snow cover typically lasts from December-April and the growing season is ~140 days (Hertel et al., 2018). Most of the landscape is low, rolling hills, 200-1000 m, covered by conifer forests of various ages and interspersed with bogs and open water. Human density in the area is low (~4-7 humans/km2), but the anthropogenic footprint is large, due to heavily managed Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) and Norway spruce (Picea abies) forests. The extensive forestry road network (~1.5 km road/km2) makes the area popular for hunting and berry picking (Steyaert et al., 2016). Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillius) is the most common berry species and covers almost 20% of the forest floor (Nilsson and Wardle 2005), though lingonberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea) and crowberry (Empetrum nigrum) are also common (Hertel et al., 2018). Sweden has one of the densest moose (Alces alces) populations in the world (Jensen et al., 2020), and invertebrates, including two genera of ants (Formica and Camponotus), are also abundant throughout the study area (Frank et al., 2015;Swenson et al., 1999). The heavily hunted bear population is very productive (Van de Walle et al., 2021a;Zedrosser et al., 2011, Swenson et al., 2017). The overall mean bear density is 30 bears/1000 km2 (Støen et al., 2005), but this varies from 0-84 bears/1000 km2 across the study area and among years (Frank et al., 2018).

div.head: Bear data
div.p: The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Bears were captured by administering an immobilizing drug via dart from a helicopter (Arnemo and Evans, 2017) in spring soon after den emergence (March through May). All capture and handling protocols were approved by the Swedish Ethical Committee on Animal

Research, Uppsala (C18/15) and the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency (NV-00741-18, NV-01758-14). While bears were anesthetized, the field crew measured the bear's skull circumference and weighed the bears while suspended below a sling scale. Most bears were known individuals first captured as yearlings with their mothers, thus age was known.

When unknown individual is were captured, a pre-molar was extracted and age was determined from counting the cementum annuli (Harshyne et al., 1998). Hair samples were collected by pulling hair from between the shoulder blades (the hump) with pliers. After collection, hair samples were placed in individual paper envelopes and stored dry at room temperature until they were processed for cortisol and stable isotope measurements. Bears are individually marked with unique numbers on their upper lip and either VHF transmitters or GPS collars.

div.head: Laboratory procedures
div.p: When processing bear hair, we removed as much underfur as possible from the sample as well as large surface contaminants, and then weighed hairs to the nearest milligram.

Preparatory procedures followed the protocol for cortisol concentration measurement (Macbeth et al., 2010) and samples for stable isotope estimation were portioned out after the grinding step (Sergiel et al., 2017).
To measure hair cortisol concentrations, we followed procedures in Macbeth et al. (2010) and a commercially available enzyme-linked immunoassay kit (Oxford EA-65 Cortisol EIA kit:

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Oxford Biomedical). In 2014, Oxford Biomedical changed the antibody they used in their kit with one that had a higher binding sensitivity, resulting in different cortisol sensitivities between the kits. Most of the between-kit variation has been corrected, thanks to published lab procedures which can correct cortisol measured with the older antibody to be like cortisol extracted with the modern antibody (Wilson et al., 2021). Intra-assay variation was 4.9% and Interassay variation was 5.1%.

To measure δ 13 C and δ 15 N, we followed Koehler et al. (2019) and used two reference materials to normalize the results to VPDB and AIR: BWBIII keratin (δ 13 C = -20.18, δ 15 N = +14.31 per mil, respectively) and PRCgel (δ 13 C = -13.64, δ 15 N= +5.07 per mil, respectively).
Within run (n = 5) precisions, as determined from both reference and sample duplicate analyses and from QA/QC controls, were ± 0.1 per mil for both δ 13 C and δ 15 N.

div.p: Question 2: How does age and reproductive state affect cortisol concentrations in this population of brown bears

We used mixed effects generalized linear regression models within a frequentist framework to explain variance in cortisol levels within our population. We used the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2014) in R (R Core Team, 2024) to fit models based on a priori hypotheses. Our cortisol data had a strong left-skew and contained values greater than zero, so we used a gamma distribution with a log-link and individual bear ID as a random effect to account for within-individual similarities. All models were compared to the intercept-only model to determine whether additional fixed effects explained more variation in the data. When comparing model fits, we used an information-theoretic framework and compared models using Akaike's second-order Information Criterion (AICc) and the difference in the AICc between models (ΔAICc) to determine the model with the best fit (Burnham & Anderson, 2000). We compared models that accounted for bear age, demographic class, and an interaction between age and demographic class. When we looked at individual effects explaining variation within the model, we determined the strength of evidence for a fixed effect by the extent to which the 95% confidence interval overlapped zero; no overlap = strong evidence, some overlap (< ~10%) = moderate evidence, and 95% confidence intervals that overlapped zero by > 15% was weak evidence for a relationship between the covariate and the response variable in the equation.

We used general mixed linear regression models within a Bayesian framework in R statistical software (R Core Team. 2004) using JAGS and the package rjags (Plummer et al., 2003) to build and compare models based on a priori hypotheses. We used four different indicators of maternal reproductive investment (offspring δ 15 N, offspring mass, and 15 N and mass transfer from mothers to offspring) as response variables. We included a year-and litter-specific family ID to account for repeated measures on the same reproducing female over multiple years and different litters. We also included a maternal ID to account for maternal-specific differences. Our fixed effects included maternal age, body condition, and δ 15 N as well as annual mean bear density, and litter size. It is well established that offspring mass is highly correlated with maternal mass (Ronget et al., 2018), as well as maternal and offspring δ 15 N values (Jenkins et al., 2001). Thus, rather than comparing models to an intercept-only model, all models were compared to a "base" model which included the intercept and either maternal mass or δ 15 N, depending on the model response variable. More complex models included additive effects and limited interactions. When comparing models to determine the model with the best fit, we used an information theoretic approach and ΔDIC values and leave-one-out cross validation to compare models (Burnham & Anderson, 2002;Gelman et al., 2013;Vehtari et al., 2017). When determining the effect of individual covariates within the models, we considered the extent to which 95% credible intervals overlapped zero (Burnham & Anderson, 2002). To determine the best model, we used an information-theoretic approach based on Akaike's second-order Information Criterion (AICc) and the difference in the criterion between candidate models (Δ AICc and the candidate model's weight (AICcw; Burnham & Anderson, 2002). If models had similar support (Δ AICc < 2), we used model averaging to derive model-averaged parameter estimates (Anderson, 2008). When we evaluated individual model terms, we systematically compared a model with and without the given term and looking at the change in the resulting AICc. We considered the model term to be informative if the 95% confidence interval did not contain zero (Arnold, 2010). Individual ID was included in all models as a random effect to account for correlation among resampled individuals. It is well established that age is highly correlated with growth (Dmitriew, 2011), therefore we used the model with the intercept and age as a "base model" and used this to compare the change in variation when other fixed effects were added. Other fixed effects included a vegetation index, study area, Julian date, whether dependent offspring were present at time of capture, and basic interactions.

div.head: Question 5: How does brown bear diet change with annual variation in resource availability
div.p: To estimate trends in brown bear diet and quantify relationships between diet and food productivity, we completed our analysis in two steps. First, we used Bayesian mixing models in R (R Core Team, 2024) and the package MixSIAR (Stock & Semmens, 2013) to derive the estimated proportions of five diet components (ants, moose, bilberry, crowberry, and lingonberry) for each demographic class (females with dependent offspring, solitary females, and solitary males) with year and bear ID as random effects. This gave us annual diet proportions for each demographic class. The next step was to use mixed effects general linear regression models in R (R Core Team, 2024) and lme4 (Bates et al., 2014) to relate the annual variation in stable isotope values and diet to annual food production. We used the

We used bear ID and reproductive category as random effects. All models were compared to the null (intercept only) model to determine if additional effects explained more variation in the data than the intercept alone. When determining the model with the best fit, we used an information theoretic framework and used Akaike's Information Criterion for small sample sizes (AICc)

and the difference in the criterion between models (Δ AICc) to determine the best model (Burnham & Anderson, 2002). When we evaluated the strength of evidence for individual model components, we considered the extent that 95% confidence intervals overlapped zero (Anderson, 2008) and the model variance for the models with and without the fixed effect being evaluated.

div.head: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
div.p: This thesis uses physiological metrics from a population of brown bears with a unique phenotype of small-bodied, highly fecund females to test several assumptions about ecological, foraging, and life-history theories.
Question 1: Do diet estimates from stable isotopes match previous estimates from scat analysis and ecological theory

Of the three foraging theories tested, brown diet most closely resembled predictions from the optimum foraging model, although none of the three models fully described the relationship between brown bear foraging and community interactions in our system. The % dry matter proportions and metabolizable energy provided by proteins in Scandinavian brown bear diet was much lower than predicted by theoretical models based on fitness (Hilderbrand et al., The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore 1999) and macronutrient balancing (Coogan et al., 2014;Erlenbach et al., 2014).

Scandinavian bears primarily consumed bilberries and lingonberries, followed by crowberries, ants, and moose. Although berries are low in nitrogen and proteins, they were the largest source of protein in the diet due to their overall large proportion of the diet. In general, we concluded that human-imposed assumptions and constraints within both theoretical and mathematical models may have resulted in a narrow view of species' diet and foraging and, therefore, their overall function within their ecological community. Despite moose making up the smallest proportion of the diet, brown bears are often referred to as "carnivore" and "apex predators" in the literature (Hertel et al., 2016;Milakovic & Parker, 2013;Morales-González et al., 2020;Niedziałkowska et al., 2019), and less often considered to be seed dispersers or competitors with other frugivores (but see García-Rodríguez et al., 2021;Harrer & Levi, 2018;Steyaert et al., 2019).

Diet and foraging are established indicators for understanding the fundamentals of ecology, from behavior, survival, reproduction, and community interactions to evolution (Darwin, 1839;MacArthur & Pianka, 1966), but separating the various contributions to fitness and their interactions is challenging. To understand these interactions, researchers rely on models, which are often overly simplistic and have specific assumptions or mathematical constraints (Evans et al., 2013;Stearns, 2000). We used brown bears to illustrate that predictions from well-established foraging theories can result in different diet and community interactions, which ultimately changes our basic understanding of individual species and ecological communities. Our results indicate that bears in our study ate less meat than predicted, which differs from accepted life history theory in this species. Specifically, carnivory is positively associated with body size and reproductive output (Zedrosser at al., 2011;Hilderbrand et al., 1996), and bears are expected to forage to maximize size and reproduction (Erlenbach et al., 2014). The optimum foraging model, however, minimizes interactions between brown bears and moose calves; yet brown bear may depredate ~25% of moose calves in our study area annually (Rauset et al., 2012;Swenson et al., 2007). Thus, none of the three models we compared to our observed brown bear diet fully described the relationship between foraging and community interactions in our system. Life histories are aggregates of complex interactions between energy acquisition and allocation, macronutrient balance, and nutrient limitations to which different species, populations, and even individuals within populations have adapted (Hilderbrand et al., 2018;Wright et al., 2019).

Acknowledging and broadening foraging theories is more likely to foster novel discoveries and insights into ecosystems than constraining species to anthropogenically imposed categories and assumptions. The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore

Cortisol is predominately a metabolic steroid hormone and reflects the energetic demands of an organisms, whether those are related to predictable day-to-day demands or noxious environmental stimuli that result in a stress response (Romero et al., 2009).

Therefore, the higher cortisol concentrations in females with dependent offspring and dependent offspring are likely related to the extraordinary metabolic demands that developing offspring and reproducing females' experience. Lactation is extremely energetically demanding (Farley & Robbins 1995;Lopéz-Alfaro et al. 2013) and may continue into the offspring's second year of life or beyond (Craighead & Mitchell, 1982;Nawaz et al., 2008). Brown bear offspring are also vulnerable to infanticide from conspecifics (Bellemain et al., 2006) and family groups may trade off quality forage for safety (Steyaert et al., 2013). Thus, overall higher cortisol concentrations in females with dependent offspring is likely related to the higher energy demands of lactation and vigilance, as well as lower diet quality. For bears in the dependent offspring category, the metabolic demands of rapid growth in the early years of life (Dahle et al., 2006) and rapid learning as they adjust to their new environment are likely reasons for greater cortisol concentrations (Grissom & Bhatnagar, 2009;Wingfield, 2013).

Maternal body size is positively associated with fitness in brown bears (Dahle et al., 2006;Hilderbrand et al., 2018) and many other taxa (Dmitriew, 2011), which creates an assumption that bigger is always better. However, local adaptations to different selection pressures may result in smaller body sizes (relative to similar populations) that represent different, but equally fit phenotypes (Ferguson & McLoughlin, 2000;Hilderbrand et al., 2018;Zamudio et al., 1995;Zedrosser et al., 2011). For example, when adult mortality is high and multiple reproductive events are uncertain, selection should favor phenotypes that reproduce early in life and invest relatively less in somatic growth and maintenance in favor of reproduction (Charlsworth et al., 1976;Pianka, 1970;Ricklefs & Wikelski, 2002).
Question 4: Are Scandinavian brown bears smaller than North American brown bears and what determines variation in growth.

Not only did brown bear size vary between the study areas, but it was also different between the sexes. Variation in female mass between the continents was best described by the model that accounted for variation in habitat and whether females had offspring or not. Alberta females were heavier and longer than Swedish females and there was a positive effect of NDVI on female size, but this effect was smaller in Sweden than in Alberta. The capture model was the most parsimonious model to explain variation in male mass between the study areas and contained no habitat variables.

In comparable boreal forest habitats in Sweden and Canada, males reach similar asymptotic body sizes. There was no support for an effect of habitat on brown bear size. Reproductive success in brown bears is dependent on body size (S. J. Arnold & Wade, 1984;Festa-Bianchet et al., 1998). Male brown bears likely have been under directional natural selection to maximize growth rate, whereas females may have different selection pressures (S. J. Arnold & Wade, 1984). This is evidenced in the effect habitat and population density had on female size. Female fecundity is strongly and positively associated with body mass across taxa (Araya-Ajoy et al., 2018;Djawdan et al., 1996;Pincheira-Donoso & Hunt, 2017) -larger individuals reproduce at younger ages and produce greater numbers of offspring of better quality (López-Alfaro et al., 2013;Robbins et al., 2012;Stearns, 1989). In direct opposition to this, we found that smaller and lighter females in Sweden had larger litters and reproduced at younger ages than the larger and heavier Alberta females.
Question 5: How does brown bear diet change with annual variation in resource availability
Posterior diet estimates for all three reproductive categories indicated that bilberries made up the greatest proportion of the diet for males, females, and females with dependent offspring.

Higher-trophic, protein-rich foods (moose and ants) made up small proportions of brown bear diets, but moose was highest in solitary adult males. Ants made up a consistently larger diet proportion in both female reproductive categories, whereas moose made up a larger proportion of the diet than ants in solitary males. Through time, there is evidence that the proportion of ants and moose in the diet have decreased, whereas the proportion of bilberry in the diet has remained stable or slightly increased. Variation in δ 13 C values was best described by log-linear relationship with bilberry productivity and the number of moose calves observed in the year in which hair was grown. δ 13 C values were lower in years in which more bilberries were produced, and more calves were observed. Variation in δ 15 N values was best described by the model that accounted for the effects of bear age, sex, an interaction

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore between age and sex, and the bilberry production index with a one-year time lag (berry production in 2007 affecting stable isotope values in 2008). δ 15 N values increased with age in both sexes, but males had higher δ 15 N values and the increase with age was much greater than in females. δ 15 Nvalues also decreased in years with higher bilberry production.

δ 13 C values were negatively correlated with both bilberry production and moose calf availability, yet these two foods are at opposite ends of the observed δ 13 C values in our system. Unexpectedly, years with greater numbers of observed moose calves were associated with brown bear δ 13 C values that were less like moose values, indicating that moose made up a lower diet proportion in years with greater numbers of reported calves.

Bears predate moose calves in the spring (Swenson et al., 2007), whereas calf observations are reported in late summer and fall (Singh et al., 2014). The association of greater proportion of moose in the diet in years of fewer reported calves may be the result of bears predating more moose calves in the spring, resulting in fewer calves to be counted in the fall.

However, from 2010 to 2014, observed moose calves rapidly increased to 3x the numbers prior to 2010, yet the proportion of moose in brown bear diet did not increase. This suggests that either moose calves are not a preferred food for bears, or calves have never been a

limited food resource within this study population. For δ 15 N values, the bilberry production in the year prior to hair growth was the best-supported food variable, indicating that primary productivity rather than prey availability drives brown bear diet. Poor bilberry production in the summer/fall may lead to bears entering dens with fewer fat reserves and, consequently, emerging in poor condition in the spring (López-Alfaro et al., 2013;Robbins et al., 2012).

Poor spring condition may result in bears with a stronger drive to replenish depleted energy stores by spending more time eating moose. Alternatively, following years of poor bilberry production, bears may not change their behavior (Hertel et al., 2019), instead, they may break down more of their own tissues, which would also result in higher δ 15 N values (Lee et al., 2012) and erroneously overestimate the proportion of moose and ants in the diet.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Although not one of the original goals of this research, this work has hopefully highlighted the importance of expanding our views of species and ecological principals beyond narrow human constructs, such as "carnivore" and "apex predator". For instance, brown bears are, by definition, apex predators because they have no natural predators. However, this does not mean that their only role in their community is as a predator that doesn't interact with the primary producers. By relaxing our model assumptions (both mathematical and theoretical)

to accommodate the complex reality we strive to understand (Evans et al., 2013;Mikkelsen et al., 2023) and allowing space for more than one solution to an evolutionary challenge (Hilderbrand et al., 2018;Liu et al., 2019), we expanded rather than confirmed our understanding of the natural world. Instead of focusing on the optimal or maximal solution to an ecological model (Mougi & Nishimura, 2009;Sinervo et al., 2000;Stearns, 1989), I suggest that the variation within and among groups may be more important (Bolnick et al., 2003;Mangel & Stamps, 2001;Urton & Hobson, 2005). Advances in ecology will come from research that seeks to push the boundaries of our knowledge and bring the fuzzy edges of our view of nature into better focus.

This thesis strived to combine this principal to look for novel answers to our five specific research questions. The overall goal of this research was to determine how energy flowed within a portion of the Swedish boreal forest ecosystem, from primary producers to an apex predator, and how this was related to physiological and life-history variation in brown bears.
We first estimated the dietary energetic contributions of both primary productivity and primary

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore consumers to the diet of brown bears (question 1) and determined that berries contributed an overwhelming proportion to the diet of our "apex predator". Secondly, we determined differences in metabolic demands among brown bears in our study population (question 2)

and found that dependent offspring and females with dependent offspring had the highest indices of metabolic demands. Reproduction is energetically costly, and in our population, meat constitutes a small proportion of the diet, and females are relatively small-bodied, yet highly fecund. Therefore, females may be resource limited and sacrificing growth to fuel reproduction, which is counter to current life-history theory for a slow pace of life species (Ricklefs & Wikelski, 2002;Wright et al., 2019). To test this, we used body condition and δ 15 N transfer from mothers to offspring to quantify maternal investment within our population (question 3) and found that even though females were smaller and less carnivorous than predicted by their reproductive output (Hilderbrand et al., 1999), there was no evidence that they were resource limited (Frank et al., 2015;Jensen et al., 2020). We found that females invest more in their own growth and maintenance than current reproduction. Growth and body size are important life-history traits and associated with fitness and reproductive output across the tree of life (Brown et al., 1993;Ronget et al., 2018), thus it is important to determine what affects growth and asymptotic body size. We used observed measurements from our brown bear population and a population in the boreal forest of North America (question 4) and determined that there was no difference in body sizes among males on the different continents, but that females in Sweden were smaller and growth between the sexes were related to different ecological drivers. Finally, because growth, reproduction, and fitness are intimately tied to resource availability (van Noordwijk & de Jong, 1986), we estimated long-term annual patterns in brown bear diet within our population and determined drivers of these patterns (question 5). Brown bear diet in our population was driven by primary productivity (bilberry production) rather than prey availability, which is surprising for an "apex predator".

One of the major themes of this research project is that the Swedish population of brown bears seems to break many of the assumptions and expectations in the literature (Erlenbach et al., 2014;Hertel et al., 2019;Hilderbrand et al., 1999) and ecological models (Denno & Fagan, 2003;MacArthur & Pianka, 1966). For instance, the historical focus in ecology on predators or carnivores as predominately secondary consumers suggests that it is unclear how many "apex predators" are sensitive to changes in primary production. Projections of changes in phenology and species distributions due to climate change (Inouye, 2022) make it critical to recognize and incorporate the direct relationships between carnivorous species and primary producers as well as prey species (Deacy et al., 2017) into our ecological models. Changes in plant phenology may affect polyphagous species in two ways: once through changes in primary producers as a food source, and secondly as prey species change in response to primary production (Deacy et al., 2017;Hertel et al., 2018;Melis et al., 2010).

As a second example, ecologists often assume that species with a slow pace of life, like brown bears, will spend resources to maximize somatic growth, because larger body size is associated with increased fitness (Brown et al., 1993;Ricklefs & Wikelski, 2002;Ronget et al., 2018). It is also assumed that small body sizes are a result of energetic limitations within the ecosystem that prevent individuals from obtaining the maximal body size (Dmitriew, 2011;Pincheira-Donoso & Hunt, 2017). Coastal brown bears which have access to large influxes of energy through salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.) spawning runs have the largest body size and highest population densities across the entire brown bear distribution (Akhremenko & Sedalishchev, 2008;López-Alfaro et al., 2015;Matsubayashi et al., 2016;Swenson et al., 2007;Zedrosser et al., 2011). As a result, coastal ecosystems are assumed to be the ideal environment for brown bears and are often used as the standard to which other populations are compared (Hilderbrand et al., 1999;Jacoby et al., 1999;Zedrosser et al., 2011).
However, this is an arbitrary comparison and minimizes the alternative point of view that no

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore single population or life history is superior to others. Rather, each iteration is a unique result from different selection pressures (Hilderbrand et al., 2018;Royauté et al., 2018). Rather than focusing on what makes one population "more fit" than the other, ecologists should focus on the environmental limitations that drive differences among individuals, populations, or species and the unique adaptations that arise due to environmental limitations.

div.head: Future Research
div.p: Understanding the diverse adaptations required to meet metabolic demands under extreme conditions and the evolutionary processes that shape and maintain these adaptations is critical to expand our comprehension of ways animals adapt to their environment, which is particularly important given the predicted increase in climate extremes (Box et al., 2019;Inouye, 2022). This research project has expanded our understanding of both brown bear ecology as well as the larger ecological theories within our discipline. Yet these are only a foundation on which to build a better understanding of life-history trade-offs in the face of extreme metabolic demands, such as giving birth and lactation during a long fast.

Results from research question 1 indicated that animal-derived foods make up a small proportion of brown bear diet, meaning their diet is lower in calories, fats, and proteins than expected. One explanation for this is that bears in this ecosystem have physiological adaptations which enable them to process berries more efficiently, making berries a higherquality food source than previously documented in other bear populations. Adaptations may include a longer gut (Chivers & Hladik, 1980;Duque-Correa et al., 2021) capable of extracting more nutrients from mast or microbiota that aid in plant matter digestion (Fontaine et al., 2018;Muegge et al., 2011;Wen et al., 2021). Investigating this would require harvesting gastro-intestinal tracts from harvested bears in Sweden and at least one other location in which to compare gut length and bacterial composition. Much of what we know

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore about bear digestion and diet is derived from a few studies on captive bears, which may not accurately represent energetic needs, food habits, or wild microbiota. A second line of inquiry would be theoretical, as we identified the shortcomings of mathematical and theoretical models which rely on optimization theory (Mougi & Nishimura, 2009;Sinervo et al., 2000) and discrete trophic levels (Chubaty et al., 2014;Kratina et al., 2012;Thompson et al., 2007).
Further research is needed to develop alternative models which are more flexible to accommodate the complex reality of natural systems.

Results from question 2 demonstrated that there was little difference in the cortisol concentrations between the sexes of solitary brown bears, though there were large differences between solitary bears and both dependent offspring and females with dependent offspring. The literature often cites male bears as having higher energetic demands due to their larger body size and this is one explanation for males being more carnivorous than female bears (Robbins et al., 2007;Welch et al., 1997). However, our results indicated that reproducing females may have higher energetic demands than solitary males, even when we account for age. This may indicate that either cortisol is not a reliable measure of metabolic demands in reproducing females, or during reproduction, females have higher metabolic demands than large-bodied males, which would predict them to be more or equally carnivorous to males. Future studies could compare metabolic demands between reproducing females and males of the same age, and females and males of the same size to determine the extent to which body size and life-history events contribute to the metabolic demands of bears and explain variations in both diet and resource demands. Social aspects, such as the trade-off between foraging and safety, would also need to be considered (Brown et al., 2023;Steyaert et al., 2013).
Research question 3 instigated several lines of further questioning regarding life-history trade-offs, as well as brown bear physiology. Our results indicated that our population

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore phenotype may be adaptive to local anthropogenic pressures, such as low adult survival from human hunting. It would be valuable to look at several aspects of human influences on demographics and how, collectively, these may change brown bear life history (Zedrosser et al., 2011) by decreasing adult survival, increasing social instability, and favoring longer interlitter intervals (Frank et al., 2017;Steyaert et al., 2016;Van de Walle et al., 2021a;2021b).

Much of this work has previously been done, but has not been synthesized into a singular, holistic study to quantify how each component contributes to life history and interacts with one another. Additionally, there is likely much individual variation in how mothers invest in reproduction (Hertel et al., 2021;Van De Walle et al., 2023). Maternal investments may be stable across litters, indicating a predetermined investment that may be genetically encoded (Pick et al., 2019). Variation may also be driven by environmental variables and litter composition, such as number and sex of offspring (Bădescu et al., 2022;Gonzalez et al., 2012). We attempted to use δ 15 N values as an indicator of maternal investment, and offspring are typically δ 15 N-enriched relative to their mothers (Jenkins et al., 2001). However, not all offspring in our study were enriched relative to their mothers. This could be an indication of family groups in which the female weaned her offspring early (Polischuk et al., 2001) or individual variation in the δ 15 N composition of milk (Reitsema et al., 2016). It would be enlightening to determine whether females who have offspring enriched in δ 15 N also invest higher proportions of energy and mass in their offspring. This would validate δ 15 N as an indicator of maternal investment. Such a study may also determine mechanisms of classic life history trade-offs, such as changing the ratio of fats and proteins mothers invest in offspring.

The results of question 5 revealed that brown bear diet seemed to respond to changes in primary productivity and that both δ 13 C and δ 15 N values in our population have distinct variances that seemed to be driven by a large-scale mechanism, likely climate. Population cycles are common in smaller mammals at high latitudes (Korpimäki et al., 2004;Krebs, The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore 1996), but are rare in large mammals. Even more rare, perhaps non-existent, is evidence of a large predatory species cycling in response to climate and primary productivity, as other predator cycles are linked to prey species (Post et al., 2002;Yan et al., 2013). Further research using climate data and better moose population data is needed to determine the origin of these cycles, which should reveal a lot about how long-lived predators can be affected by climate. This is important for future species conservation under climate change, not only for bears, but other polyphagous species as well. It would also be important to include physiological indicators of health, such as body condition and cortisol, to determine if there is not only a dietary shift, but also a physiological response to changes in primary productivity. This will help us determine if bears fully compensate for years with poor bilberry production or if they catabolize stored reserves to make up their energetic deficit. Results from question 5 also showed a distinct increase in δ 15 N with age, especially in males. This may be related to increasing carnivory with increasing size and age, but evidence shows that females predate almost, if not equal, numbers of moose calves as male bears (Ballard et al., 1990;Keay et al., 2018;Rauset et al., 2012;Swenson et al., 2007). It may also be that older, larger males are more infanticidal than younger males (Bellemain et al., 2006;Hrdy, 1979), and the very different δ 15 N values may be driven by males consuming killed bear cubs, however, data on instances of infanticide and cannibalism are relatively rare. One way to determine this would be to model diets that slowly increase in prey-derived proportions and separately model diets with increasing proportions of bear cubs to replicate our observed pattern and determine whether this is biologically feasible. Negative results would indicate that there may be secondary physiological differences between males and females that result in these differences.

This research highlighted under-valued community interaction between an apex predator and primary production. As researchers, we need to be acutely aware of how the language we use when describing species can affect how we formulate research questions, interpret

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore results and influence the next researcher who reads our work. When we consider carnivores as simple predators or down-grade the non-animal derived proportions of the diet, we also downgrade those community interactions, which may be very important. We should also strive to remember that evolution selecting phenotypes which maximize fitness is a human construct to explain the vast variation on life that we observe. Aberrations from expected norms should be viewed as possible alternate, yet equally adaptive strategies, rather than sub-optimal phenotypes. Further research that builds on the findings of this research project will expand our understanding of these alternate strategies that animals use to survive and reproduce in a world of limited resources

We also developed three hypotheses based on predominant foraging literature, and then compared predicted diets to field estimates. Our three models assumed 1) bears forage to optimize caloric efficiency (optimum foraging model), predicting bears predominately eat berries (~70% of diet) and opportunistically feed on moose (Alces alces) and ants (Formica spp. and Camponotus spp; ~15% each); 2) bears maximize meat intake (maximizing fitness model), predicting a diet of 35-50% moose, followed by ants (~30%), and berries (~15%); 3) bears forage to optimize macronutrient balance (macronutrient model), predicting a diet of ~22% (dry weight) or 17% metabolizable energy from proteins, with the rest made up of carbohydrates and lipids (~ 49% and 29% dry matter or 53% and 30% metabolizable energy, respectively). Bears primarily consumed bilberries (Vaccinium myrtillus; 50-55%), followed by lingonberries (V.

vitis-idaea; 22-30%), crowberries (Empetrum nigrum; 8-15%), ants (5-8%), and moose (3-4%). Dry matter dietary protein was lower than predicted by the maximizing fitness model and the macronutrient balancing model, but protein made up a larger proportion of the metabolizable energy than predicted. While diets most closely resembled predictions from optimal foraging theory, none of the foraging hypotheses fully described the relationship between foraging and ecological niche in brown bears. Acknowledging and broadening models based on foraging theories is more likely to foster novel discoveries and insights into the role of polyphagous species in ecosystems and we encourage this approach.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Many ecological principles are built on theoretical relationships connecting diet, space use, and fitness (Darwin, 1839;MacArthur & Pianka 1966). However, determining such relationships in practice is complicated, as fitness is a complex function of both physiological and environmental constraints that vary among individuals and populations, while diet varies seasonally, across life-history stages, and among individuals. Researchers are typically

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore forced to use imperfect models with specific assumptions and mathematical constraints to test, interpret, and predict ecological community structure and interactions (Evans et al., 2013;Stearns, 2000). Thus, our understanding of a species' ecological niche, from theoretical underpinnings to conclusions drawn are affected by assumptions and biases.

Most foraging models use mathematical optimization theory, which not only has a suite of assumptions, but changing optimization targets leads to different predicted diets, which may alter predicted landscape use, and ultimately, expectations about an organism's ecological niche (Garay et al., 2012;Houston & McNamara, 2014). For instance, researchers from different ecological disciplines typically concentrate on specific aspects of foraging strategies which can lead to distinct, narrow conclusions (Houston & McNamara, 2014). While physiologists may estimate the health implications of nutritionally imbalanced diets (Erlenbach et al., 2014), evolutionary biologists concentrate on ways animals forage to maximize reproductive output (Hilderbrand et al., 1999), and general optimal foraging theory uses energetic (typically caloric) efficiency to explain foraging decisions (MacArthur & Pianka 1966). When considering diet optimization, a physiologist may require food to be available ad libitium to determine baseline nutritional needs of a species, while a behavioral ecologist likely assumes organisms exist in patchy environments in which optimized diets can only be realized under the constraints of a natural environment.

Shifting targets of how we quantify animal foraging and corresponding inferences that result makes broad ecological understanding of ecological communities difficult. This is particularly true for species with large distributions or which use diverse resources, such as polyphagous species (Loxdale & Harvey, 2023;Richmond et al., 2005). Brown bears (Ursus arctos) have a large circumpolar distribution and use a variety of landscapes and foods (Bojarska & Selva, 2012;Diserens et al., 2020). Although, taxonomically, brown bears are carnivores, most populations consume little meat; relying on vegetation, hard and soft mast, and invertebrates (Bojarska & Selva, 2012;Diserens et al., 2020). However, meat is the most efficiently

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore digested food in brown bear diets (Pritchard & Robbins, 1990) and greater carnivory in brown bears is positively associated with population density, body size, and reproductive output (Hilderbrand et al., 1999;Mowat & Heard, 2006;Zedrosser et al., 2006), partially due to greater fixed nitrogen and energy density at higher trophic levels (Elser et al., 2000). Thus, carnivory is generally assumed to be the ideal foraging niche for brown bears, (Costello et al., 2016;Erlenbach et al., 2014;Hilderbrand et al., 1999;López-Alfaro et al., 2015;Mowat & Heard, 2006). Yet, the variability of brown bear foraging makes it difficult to draw broad conclusions between diet, body size, and fitness, as some populations of brown bears maintain high reproductive output despite small body sizes and realtively low carnivory (Zedrosser et al., 2011). For this reason, we prefer the term polyphagous to carnivore or omnivore (Loxdale & Harvey, 2023).

Much of the theory on brown bear diet comes from North American coastal populations with access to salmon, which is high in fat and may confound the relationship between meat and fitness (Gende et al., 2001;Hilderbrand et al., 1999;Mowat & Heard 2006;López-Alfaro et al., 2015). In contrast, brown bears in Sweden feed predominately on moose (Alces alces), ants (Formica spp. and Camponotus spp.), and berries (primarily Vaccinium and Empetrum species), but the proportions of each diet component varies both seasonally and annually (Dahle et al., 1998;Persson et al., 2001;Stenset et al., 2016). Sweden has one of the highest moose densities in the world and moose are heavily harvested (Jensen et al., 2020), creating many oportunities for bears to scavenge moose carcasses and prey on calves in the spring (Rauset et al., 2012;Stenset et al., 2016;Swenson et al., 2007). In summer, brown bears become largely frugivorous (Dahle et al., 1998;Persson et al., 2001;Stenset et al., 2016), and though they are patchily distributed, berries in Scandinavian forests are numerous (Bohlin et al., 2021), providing a predictable food source (Hertel et al., 2016(Hertel et al., , 2018;;Stenset et al., 2016). Throughout their active season, bears also consume ants, but foraging peaks in mid-summer after the moose calving season, but before berries are widely

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore available (Stenset et al., 2016). Ants are abundant in Sweden (Swenson et al., 1999;Frank et al., 2015), but the numbers of pupae vary seasonally, changing the overall caloric value of ants as a food (Swenson et al., 1999).

Brown bears in Sweden have a reproductive output associated with a diet of ~77% meat (Hilderbrand et al., 1999;McLellan, 2011;Zedrosser et al., 2011), which would be twice the meat consumption estimated previously (Dahle et al., 1998;Persson et al., 2001;Stenset et al., 2016). Assuming that bears maximize meat intake to maximize reproductive output (maximizing fitness model), bears should predominately consume vulnerable moose calves in the spring and scavenge moose carcasses whenever available, and then bears should favor ants to maintain protein and energy intake (Hilderbrand et al., 1999;Mowat & Heard 2006), while berries should be consumed minimally (Coogan et al., 2014;Erlenbach et al., 2014). Under the maximizing fitness model, bears should be major predators of the vertebrate community, minimally interact with the plant community, and be sensitive to future changes in prey populations.

In contrast to maximizing meat consumption, many foraging models use overall caloric efficiency as the diet component to be optimized (optimum foraging model), which predicts that bears in Sweden should favor foraging on berries over moose. Scandinavia's history of intensive silviculture (Östlund et al., 1997) has created a landscape in which berries are abundant, while moose and ants are distributed more sporadically across the landscape (Rauset et al., 2012;Swenson et al., 1999). Berries are less digestible and less energy dense than ants and moose (3.04 kcal/g vs. 4.77 and 5.13 kcal/g, respectively), yet their availability and ease of capture relative to moose and ants makes them more energetically economical and therefore, the best food source (MacArthur & Pianka, 1966). The optimum foraging model predicts brown bears to be minor predators of vertebrates and ants (likely

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore only opportunistically) and strong interactions with the plant community, likely sensitive to changes in berry production.

Rather than assume an organism seeks to optimize a single currency, such as caloric efficiency or meat, organisms may forage to balance multiple currencies (Coogan et al., 2014;Houston & McNamara, 2014;Erlenbach et al., 2014) such as an ideal macronutrient ratio (balancing macronutrient model; Erlenbach et al., 2014;Raubenheimer et al., 2009).

Feeding experiments offer a way to specifically measure the ratio of macronutrients animals prefer, and captive brown bears select a diet of approximately 22% dry matter protein, 17% metabolizable energy content from protein, and 78% dry matter or 70% energy from nonprotein sources, with bears preferring lipids over carbohydrates (Erlenbach et al., 2014).

Food that provides predominately one macronutrient, such as berries and moose meat, are low-quality foods whereas, ants, which offer more-balanced ratios of proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids, are higher quality (Raubenheimer et al., 2009; Appendix S1: Table S1). Under the balancing macronutrient model, bears should predominantly consume ants and, to a lesser extent, moose to meet protein demands and then use berries to meet energetic demands while avoiding protein over-consumption (Erlenbach et al., 2014;Robbins et al., 2022;Rode et al., 2021). This model predicts brown bears are major predators of ants, minor predators of moose, and moderately interact with the plant community.

In addition to biases imposed by assumptions associated with chosen foraging targets and model constraints, field methods to estimate diet, such as observation, scat and gut content analyses, or cafeteria-style feeding experiments, also have inherent biases and assumptions that can affect results and inferences (Tieszen & Boutton, 1989). Further, many of these methods cannot explain how organisms assimilate ingested foods into new tissues (Tieszen & Boutton, 1989). A carnivore or polyphagous species may regularly ingest plants, but an important distinction is whether this is done to aid gut transit or build new tissues (Leigh et The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore al., 2018). Naturally occurring stable isotope values of tissues are related to the assimilated diet and can be used to estimate the proportions of isotopically unique foods used by animals (Chamberlain et al., 2005;Felicetti et al., 2003;Koehler et al., 2019;Tieszen & Boutton, 1989).

A clear understanding of an organism's foraging behavior is essential to defining ecological interactions, while understanding energy allocation is vital to describing life history and how animals respond to future environmental perturbations or long-term changes. The goal of this study was to use stable isotope (δ 13 C, δ 15 N) measurements to estimate dietary proportions of five foods in brown bear diet and to compare these estimates to those reported in earlier conventional (i.e. scat analyses) studies on the same population. We also aimed to compare the diet of bears in southcentral Sweden to other populations throughout their range. Brown bears were also used as a model species to illustrate how theoretical assumptions, model constraints, and different optimization targets result in different predicted diets, as well as ecological niches. We used published papers on brown bear ecology from across their range (Bojarska & Selva, 2012;Craighead and Mitchell, 1982;Hilderbrand et al., 1999;Jacoby et al., 1999;Pritchard & Robbins, 1990;Stenset et al., 2016;Swenson et al., 1999;Zedrosser et al., 2006Zedrosser et al., , 2011) ) to develop three foraging hypotheses within the framework of optimal foraging, maximizing fitness, and balancing macronutrients. We then compared predicted diet to observed estimated diet to determine how well foraging theories described behavior of wild populations. Assuming bears forage to maximize fitness, meat should make up 35-50%

of their diet, with ants and berries making up the rest (~30% and ~15% respectively). Under the optimal foraging model, bears should predominantly consume berries (~70%) and opportunistically feed on moose and ants (~15% each). Finally, under the balancing macronutrients model, bears will have mixed diets that will vary in food sources but result in ~22% protein and 78% non-protein sources, with more lipids than carbohydrates (Figure 1).
