div.head: MATERIALS AND METHODS
div.p: Our study area encompassed ~13,000 km In brown bears, hair growth begins in late April and continues into October, with quiescent phase over winter, but the actual growth phase varies by individual (Cattet et al., 2018;Jacoby et al., 1999;Jimbo et al., 2020). Bears in this study were captured in the spring and we used many homogenized guard hairs, thus collected hair samples represented diet from the entire previous active season, from the moose calving to berry season (Dahle et al., 1998;Persson et al., 2001;Rode et al., 2016;Stenset et al., 2016). While hair is a proteinbased tissue, carbon in hair can be derived from all sources within the diet.
When processing brown bear hair, we only used guard hairs and removed visible surface contaminants, then weighed hairs to the nearest milligram. Preparatory procedures followed

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore the protocol for cortisol concentration measurement (Macbeth et al., 2010) and samples for stable isotope assay were portioned out after the grinding step (Sergiel et al., 2017; Appendix S1). We washed each sample three times with 40 μl HPLC grade methanol per mg hair for 3 min per wash to remove other external contaminants (Sergiel et al., 2020). After the hair had dried for at least 24 hours, it was ground to a fine powder in a mixer mill (Retsch MM4000; Retsch GmbH, Germany) at 30 Hz and then put into plastic vials. To measure δ 13 C and δ 15 N in hair, we followed and PRCgel (δ 13 C = -13.64‰, δ 15 N= +5.07‰, respectively). Within run (n = 5) precisions as determined from both reference and sample duplicate analyses and from QA/QC controls were ± 0.1‰ for both δ 13 C and δ 15 N.

To estimate dietary proportions, we used stable isotope values from the five main bear foods in the study area: bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus), crowberry (Empetrum nigrum), lingonberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea), ants, and moose. In 2016, berry and ant samples were collected from within the study area. To determine the proportion of moose in the diet, we used moose hairs collected from local wild moose. We used nutritional information from previous bear studies and the USDA National Nutrient Database (Coogan et al., 2014;Erlenbach et al., 2014;Swenson et al., 1999;USDA, 2018) to estimate the percent protein, carbohydrates, and fat in brown bear diets (Appendix S1: Table S1).
Prior to analysis, we corrected δ 13 C values for the anthropogenic depletion of 13 C in the atmosphere caused by fossil fuel combustion (Seuss effect) by applying a -0.022‰

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore correction per year (Chamberlain et al., 2005) and derived source-specific trophic discrimination factors to convert prey δ 13 C and δ 15 N values to hair equivalent values (Appendix S1). Then, we graphed our consumers and food sources in isotopic bivariate space to ensure that bears in our study fell within the mixing polygon and that each endpoint was isotopically distinct (Figure 2; Phillips et al., 2014). Based on the isotopic mixing space (Figure S1) the ant and moose dietary endpoints were isotopically similar, as were those of crowberry and lingonberry, indicating the model was unable to distinguish between them.

However, we decided to group end-members a posteriori rather than a priori (Parnell et al., 2013;Phillips et al., 2014). For final diet estimations, we used the package simmr (Parnell, 2013) with uninformative priors (Appendix S1: Table S4) and four chains for 1,000,000 iterations, a burn-in of 500,000, and a thinning rate of 500. Initial values were randomly generated. We accounted for concentration dependency in the model by including the % carbon and nitrogen of each food source (Phillips & Koch, 2002; Appendix S1: Table S5).

Following Erlenbach et al. (2014) and Coogan et al. (2014), we used the posterior mean dietary proportions calculated from the mixing models and published macronutrient contents for each food group (ants, berries, and moose) to calculate the % dry matter and % metabolizable energy of lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates in the diet (Appendix S1: Tables S1 andS7).

div.head: RESULTS
div.p: We analysed hair samples from 378 individuals collected during 1995-2015. Our data contained 840 unique bear-year combinations (Appendix S1: Table S6) to estimate dietary proportions of the five main foods for brown bears in southcentral Sweden. After the application of trophic discrimination factors and accounting for concentration dependence, the model partially differentiated between the ant and moose endpoints, as well as the three

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore berry endpoints. Ants and moose estimates had a correlation of -0.74 while crowberry and lingonberry had a correlation of -0.79. A negative correlation among source estimates indicates that the sources are too similar to be confidently estimated separately and increasing the proportion of one food results in a corresponding decrease of the negatively correlated source. For example, given the error around the estimates of ants and moose, there was evidence that ants made up a greater proportion than moose, but the exact proportion of the two correlated foods cannot be precisely determined. However, the resulting diet estimates did not overlap (Figure 3), and though we calculated separate berry proportions, when deriving inferences, berries were considered as a single category, therefore we did not combine diet sources a priori.

Bears in our population primarily consumed bilberries (50-55%), followed by lingonberries (22-30%), crowberries (8-15%), ants (5-8%), and moose (3-4%; Figure 3). Among berry species, dietary proportions mirrored nitrogen content, with bilberry having the greatest nitrogen content (0.81%) followed by lingonberry (0.64%), and crowberry with the lowest nitrogen content (0.42%; Tables S1 andS6).

When we considered the % dry matter macronutrient proportions and % metabolizable energy, proteins in the diet were well below predictions from the maximizing fitness model (~13% observed vs ~ 40-50% predicted) and less than predicted by the balancing macronutrients model (predicted: 22% dry matter and 17% metabolizable energy, observed:

13% dry matter and 12% metabolizable energy; Table 1). Though berries are low in proteins, due to their large proportion of the diet, they were the largest source of protein. Observed brown bear diet was also lower in lipids than predicted by the balancing macronutrients model.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: Diet and resource acquisition have long been standard measures for understanding behavior, survival, reproduction, community interactions and evolution (Darwin, 1839;MacArthur & Pianka, 1966). We used brown bears to illustrate that even within a well-studied species, application of models that use different foraging targets or strategies can result in different predicted diets, behaviors, and niches, which affects our fundamental understanding of ecology. Our results using a simple bulk stable-carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis indicate that bears in our study ate less proteins, fats, and meat than predicted. This finding differs from accepted life history theory in this species, specifically, the relationship between carnivory, body size, and reproductive output. More specific studies that analyse a larger suite of elements or use specific amino acids might be able to differentiate between bulk foods that were isotopically similar in this system (Whiteman et al., 2019). That approach may provide a more precise understanding of metabolic routing. In addition, our results emphasize areas within foraging ecology that could be improved to further our understanding of basic ecology. Many of the ecological and mathematical assumptions within our models may have limited the scope and depth of ecological inferences. Below, we highlight some of these limitations and proposed modifications.

Our estimated brown bear diets were lower in meat and protein than predicted under the maximizing fitness or balancing macronutrients model. Diet greater than one-third meat, as estimated from previous scat analyses, would indicate that brown bears were consuming protein quantities more like obligate carnivores, such as felids, rather than other polyphagous species (Clauss et al., 2010). Protein overconsumption is linked to kidney and liver disease, as well as increased risk of cancer (Delimaris, 2013;Robbins et al., 2022;Rode et al., 2021).
One issue related to estimating protein in diets of wild animals is that estimates often cannot differentiate between skeletal muscle, which is high in protein and deficient in fats and

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore carbohydrates, and viscera, which has a more-balanced macronutrient content (USDA, 2018). Often, both skeletal muscle and viscera are collectively referred to as "meat" (Felicetti et al., 2003;Hilderbrand et al., 1996;Hobson et al., 2000;Mizukami et al., 2005), despite their macronutrient differences and a consumer's ability to preferentially consume one over the other (Gende et al., 2001;Towner et al., 2022).

Predictions from the optimal foraging model best resembled estimates from stable isotope analysis of hair whereby berries constituted most of the diet (~89%) while ants and moose made up small proportions during hair growth (~7% and 4%, respectively). Even combined as a single nitrogen source, moose and ants account for 11% ± 0.3% of the diet, indicating that nitrogen-rich foods made up a small portion of the energy budget. From these results, we might conclude that brown bears in southcentral Sweden are weak predators of moose,

given that moose make up only a small portion of brown bear diet. Yet bears prey on a large proportion of moose calves born annually (~25%; Rauset et al., 2012;Swenson et al., 2007), and thus the optimum foraging model likely underestimates the interaction between moose and brown bears. Brown bear predation on moose varies by individual (Rauset et al., 2012;Swenson et al., 2007), which was also indicated in the variation of hair δ 15 N values within our population (Supplementary Materials; Figure 1). Thus, we do not expect all predators to exert uniform predation pressure on their prey, nor do we expect all predators to respond uniformly to changes in a given prey population (Bolnick et al., 2003).

Based solely on the isotopic analysis of hair, our study could not account for individual variation or seasonal changes in diet. Bear hair grows from late April to October, but growing periods vary considerably (Cattet et al., 2018;Jacoby et al., 1999;Jimbo et al., 2020), and hair is not a completely inert tissue. Bears in our study tend to consume more protein-rich foods during the breeding season (May -July), which coincides with the moose calving season, but during this time bears spend little time foraging (Stenset et al., 2016;Swenson et The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore al., 2007). This variation in seasonal diets by bears presents a challenge to inferences derived from any method used to estimate diets, unless researchers use repeated sampling or a suite of tissues representing different periods of dietary integration. Hair overwhelmingly represents a protein metabolic pathway (i.e., all nitrogen in hair is derived from proteins in diet or body tissue and not from lipids or carbohydrates). However, carbon in hair can be derived from all three macronutrients. We attempted to account for macromolecular compositions of diets based on a largely protein-based mixing model (in turn dependent on δ15N measurements in the mixing model) and our isotopic discrimination factors were specific to both plant and animal diets. In addition, the exact proportions of each food in the diet could not be precisely estimated in our analysis, because the moose and ant endmembers had similar isotopic signatures. Moose and ant endpoints were negatively correlated (-0.74), yet this alone does not make our results uninformative (Parnell et al., 2013). While we did not determine the dietary proportions of ants vs. moose, it is clear from the posterior distribution that ants made up a larger proportion of the diet than moose (Figure 3). Given the narrow range of estimates (ants: 5-8%, moose: 3-4%) and low variation (ants SD = .06%, moose SD =.04%), even assuming the highest proportion of moose (12% of diet with 0% ants) the overall % dry matter content of protein only increased by ~3%. A diet of 12% moose and 0% ants is still much lower in protein than predicted from captive feeding trials (16-28% predicted dry matter protein content vs ~12.5% observed and 13-21%

predicted % energetic content of protein vs ~11.5% observed). Thus, our conclusions regarding brown bear foraging targets and the effects of model assumptions remain unchanged, despite isotopic similarities between these two food types.

Our understanding of animal diet and foraging ecology remains incomplete, due in part to biases within our theoretical and methodological frameworks (Mougi & Nishimura, 2008;Stearns, 2000). For instance, within community ecology, until recently models have neglected polyphagous species (Thompson et al., 2007), assuming they are rare,

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore destabilizing members of food webs (Chubaty et al., 2014;Gutgesell et al., 2022). This assumption biased early research into categorizing species within a fixed dichotomy of carnivory vs. herbivory separated by discrete trophic levels (Chubaty et al., 2014). However, polyphagy is prevalent in varying degrees across taxa, trophic levels, and ecosystems (Chubaty et al., 2014;Thompson et al., 2007). Models that relax the foundational ecological assumptions, such as carnivore-herbivore dichotomies, fixed trophic levels, stable equilibria, and organisms as perfect consumers, can explain realized, complex ecological communities better than simplified, rigid models (Mougi & Nishimura, 2008;Stearns, 2000).

Even though modern nutritional ecology models use macronutrient balance as their optimization targets (Coogan et al., 2014;Raubenheimer et al., 2009;Rode et al., 2021), determining "optimal" macronutrient balance often comes from cafeteria-style feeding experiments in laboratory or zoo settings (Erlenbach et al., 2014;Felicetti et al., 2003).

These studies may have limited application to wild populations because they do not account for search and handling time or changing availability on the landscape. Macronutrient content of wild brown bear diets differed from predictions from captive feeding trials, which is likely related to the search and handling time of high-protein foods in our system and inherently different metabolic demands for free-ranging bears, rather than evidence that macronutrient balance is not important to brown bears. Berries are also assumed to be low in lipids, yet many species, including two in this study, are rich in fatty acids (Klavins et al., 2019).
Therefore, moose offal and berries may contribute more lipids than we estimated.

Diets of Scandinavian brown bears contained less meat and protein than predicted from the maximizing fitness and balancing macronutrient models. Even though annual diets most closely resembled predictions from the optimum foraging model, none of the three models fully described the relationship between foraging and community interactions in our system.

In general, herbivorous diets may not be as protein limited as historically thought and over-consuming protein has negative health consequences for polyphagous species (Robbins et al., 2022;Rode et al., 2021;Rothman et al., 2011). Life histories are aggregates of complex interactions between energy acquisition and allocation, macronutrient balance, and nutrient limitations to which different species, populations, and even individuals within populations have adapted. Acknowledging and broadening foraging theories is more likely to foster novel discoveries and insights into ecosystems than constraining behavior to anthropogenically imposed categories and assumptions. Future studies should carefully consider the explicit and implicit assumptions contained in theories and models we apply to ecological studies and loosen assumptions to accommodate the dynamic and cryptic relationships often missed in narrow ecological studies. div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Allostasis is the concept of maintaining a stable balance of energetic incomes and costs through both predictable life history events, like reproduction, and unpredictable events that may result in chronic stress (Wingfield, 2005). Energy expenditure is mediated partly through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA), which excretes glucocorticoids in response to metabolic demands (Sapolsky 2000). At baseline concentrations, these hormones are involved in the immune response, water balance, and various metabolic pathways (MacDougall-Shackleton et al. 2019;Sapolsky 2000). Concentration increases in response to noxious stimuli, activating secondary physiological pathways, known as the "vertebrate stress response" (Sapolsky, 2000) in which these hormones reallocate energy away from long-term fitness investments like immunity and reproduction (Landys et al. 2006;Sapolsky 2000) and shift resources towards immediate survival (Wingfield and Kitaysky 2002).

Long-term chronic stress is defined as the long-term activation of an animal's HPA axis caused by unpredictable or uncontrollable stimuli (stressors) in its environment (Boonstra 2013). Stress responses enable animals to cope with challenges in the face of both environmental certainty and uncertainty (Sheriff et al. 2011). The chronic stress response of wild animals commonly depends on ecological factors such as interspecific competition (e.g., Filacorda et al. 2022;Franchini et al. 2023), habitat quality and fragmentation (Rangel-Negrín

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore et al. 2009;Franchini et al. 2019;Horcajada-Sánchez et al. 2019), human disturbance (Piñeiro et al. 2012;Zwijacz-Kozica et al. 2013;Klich et al. 2020). Life), as well as life history traits, such as sex, social or reproductive status, and age (Heimbürge et al. 2019). Some glucocorticoids, such as cortisol, may decline with age (González-de-la-Vara et al. 2011;Comin et al. 2012;Montillo et al. 2014) or among age classes, with higher cortisol concentrations typically higher in subadults compared to adults (Dettmer et al. 2014;Fourie et al. 2016). This may be caused by higher metabolic costs linked to growth and development (Comin et al. 2012;González-de-la-Vara et al. 2011;Montillo et al. 2014).

Stress hormones commonly differ between the sexes in mammals (e.g., Azevedo et al. 2019;Shell et al. 2017;Tilbrook et al. 2017;Terwissen 2000). Pregnant females generally show higher cortisol levels as cortisol is important for fetal organ maturation and the induction of parturition (Heimbürge et al. 2019). After offspring are born, they tend to have higher cortisol levels due to the energetic costs linked to rearing offspring (Mislan et al. 2016;Cattet et al. 2018), such as lactation (Arnould & Ramsay 1994;Derocher et al. 1993).

Cortisol can be measured in different matrices such as blood (Ventrella et al. 2020), or urine (e.g., Rehbinder & Hau 2006;Zbyryt et al. 2018). However, hair cortisol concentrations (HCCs) provide an estimate of circulating cortisol concentrations over a longer period and is more stable than other matrices (MacBeth et al., 2010;Prandi et al. 2018). During the active hair growth phase, cortisol is accumulated in the hair shaft via passive diffusion from blood vessels (Meyer & Novak 2012). Consequently, the individual HPA axis activity over weeks to even years can be measured in hair (Macbeth et al. 2010;Meyer & Novak 2012), and its long-term measurements across different age and reproductive classes can help to understand the physiological demands of a species.
Here we use the brown bear (Ursus arctos), a solitary-living omnivore, as a model species to study the relationship between long-term measurements of cortisol in hair and life history

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore traits, i.e., solitary bears vs females with dependent offspring vs offspring accompanying mothers. Research on congeneric polar bears (U. maritimus) suggested effects of age (Mislan et al. 2016) and social status (Macbeth et al. 2012;Mislan et al. 2016) on long-term HPA axis activity. In comparison, there may be a negative (Cattet et al. 2018) or no associations between HCC and age in brown bears (MacBeth et al., 2010). We hypothesize that rearing offspring is costly and causes increased levels of HCC (Alekseeva et al. 2020;Heimbürge et al. 2019). High energetic and/or nutritional costs linked to lactation can lead to higher cortisol concentrations in mothers (Arnould & Ramsay 1994;Cattet et al. 2018;Derocher et al. 1993). We therefore predict 1) higher HCC concentrations in females with dependent offspring compared to solitary males and females. We further hypothesize that offspring accompanying mothers have higher energetic demands than solitary adults and ultimately higher cortisol levels due to the costs linked to rapid growth (Dahle et al. 2006).
We therefore predict 2) higher HCC concentrations in offspring accompanying mothers compared to solitary males and females.

div.head: Study area
div.p: The study area was in southcentral Sweden (61°N, 15°E), covers approximately 13,000 km², and is characterized by bogs, lakes, and managed coniferous forests. The terrain is hilly, with elevations ranging from 200 to 850 meters. The area is predominantly (~80%) covered by intensively managed boreal forests of different ages 0 to 100 years (Swenson et al. 1999), and mainly composed of Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris), Norway spruce (Picea abies), and birch (Betula spp; Moe et al. 2007). Heather (Calluna vulgaris), grasses, and berry-producing shrubs dominate the understory vegetation, while bogs and lakes occupy the remaining area.

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Precipitation ranges between 350 and 450 mm during the vegetation period, and snow cover lasts from approximately November until the end of April/early May (Elfström et al. 2008).
Human density is low at 1-7 inhabitants/km2, but the landscape is crisscrossed by gravel roads with a density of approximately 1 ± 0.5 km/km2 (Martin et al. 2010;Ordiz et al. 2014).

Human presence is highest during summer and autumn, primarily due to hunting, as well as berry and mushroom picking (Martin et al. 2010). The population density of bears in the study area is ~23 individuals per 1,000 km2 (Bischof et al. 2009). Brown bears in Sweden are legally hunted from 21 August -15 October or until quotas are filled, and around 10% are harvested from the total population annually (Bischof et al. 2009).

div.head: Sample collection and laboratory analysis
div.p: Bears were captured as part of an individual-based long-term monitoring project by remote drug delivery from a helicopter shortly after leaving the den from 1990 to 2016 (e.g., Swenson et al. 2001;Zedrosser et al. 2013;Arnemo & Evans 2017). We did not capture cubs-of-the-year for ethical reasons. Offspring in family groups were captured for the first time as yearlings (Zedrosser et al. 2013;Arnemo & Evans 2017). In many cases, bear age was known because offspring of radio-collared females were followed from the year of birth (Swenson et al. 2001;Zedrosser et al. 2013). In cases in which year of birth was unknown, age was estimated by counting the cementum annuli of an extracted premolar (Matson et al. 1993) Hair samples were collected during capture with pliers from between the shoulder blades, then air-dried and stored in the dark at room temperature until further analysis (Sergiel et al.

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore 2020). Prior to cortisol extraction, we removed as much underfur and debris from guard hairs as possible, and then weighed the sample to the nearest milligram. We followed the procedures in Macbeth et al. (2010) and Sergiel et al. (2020) by first washing each hair sample a total of three times in 40 µL HPLC grade methanol per mg hair for three minutes.

After drying the hair for at least 24 hours, we used a mixer mill (Retsch MM4000; Retsch GmbH, Germany) at 30 Hz to grind each hair sample to a fine powder. This powder was placed in plastic tubes with 0.5 mL HPLC grade methanol and gently vortexed for 10 seconds. Samples were then placed on a rotator at low speed for 24 hours and then centrifuged for 15 minutes at 4500 revolutions/minute. We collected the supernatant and transferred it to a 12 mm glass test tube, then used two replications of additional washings in 0.5 mL of fresh methanol, vortexed for another 15 minutes at 4500 revolutions per minute and collected the resulting supernatant. The three supernatants were pooled and dried under nitrogen gas at 38C. Dried steroid hormones were reconstituted in 0.2 mL of phosphate buffer for 12 hours at 4C. We vortexed reconstituted samples on a low setting for 40 seconds, transferred to 1.5 mL plastic vials, then centrifuged for 15 minutes at 4500 revolutions per minute. We then analyzed 50 µL aliquots with an enzyme linked immunoassay kit from Oxford Biomedical (Rochester Hills, MI, USA) and standardized extracted HCC to hair mass. Extracts were run in duplicates to calculate intra-and interassay variation of 4.9% and 5.1%, respectively (Macbeth et al. 2010;Sergiel et al. 2020).

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: HCC variations in relation to age and social status were analyzed using generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) with a Gamma distribution and a log-link function to accommodate positive date with a left-hand skew. We used HCC as the response variable, age and social status as fixed factors, and bear ID as random factor to account for the autocorrelation among repeated measurements of individuals among years (i.e., recaptures). We chose not

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore to include mass into the analyses because it is highly correlated with age in brown bears (Zedrosser et al. 2006;Swenson et al. 2007). We compared the model structure of an intercept-only model (i.e., null model) with the most complex model (i.e., the one containing the interaction between fixed factors) and another model in which only the additive effect between fixed factors was considered. We tested for multicollinearity among fixed factors using the variance inflation factor (VIF) implemented in the 'car' package (Fox & Weisberg 2019). VIFs ≥ 5 were considered as threshold values to define high correlation among predictors (Akinwande et al. 2015) and these factors were not included in the same model.

The selection of the most parsimonious model was based on Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample sizes (AICc; Hurvich & Tsai 1989). We used the 'blme' package (Chung et al. 2013) in the statistical software R 4.3.1 (R Development Core Team 2023) for all statistical analyses.

div.head: RESULTS
div.p: We used HCCs from 693 hair samples collected from 370 individuals, aged one to nine years old, captured from one to eight times during 1990-2016 (Table 1). Among females, we had 61 females sampled with dependent offspring sampled 1-2 times, and 81 solitary females sampled 1-7 times. Females can appear in both categories in different years and our dataset contained 30 females that were sampled both as solitary females and females with dependent offspring.

The highest HCCs were observed in dependent offspring (mean = 6.83 ± 3.02 (SD) pg/mg; median = 5.70 pg/mg; range = 2.32 -15.59 pg/mg), followed by mothers with dependent offspring (mean = 6.66 ± 4.17 pg/mg; median = 5.08 pg/mg; range = 2.70 -27.41 pg/mg), solitary females (mean = 5.50 ± 3.72 pg/mg; median = 4.45 pg/mg; range = 2.19 -31.33

The GLMM best explaining the variation in HCC included the fixed effects of age and social status as well as the interaction between age and social status (Figure 1; Table 3). HCC did not increase significantly with age in mothers, solitary females, and solitary males, however, dependent two-year-old offspring had significantly lower HCC compared to dependent yearling offspring (Figure 2; Table 3).

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: We found that mothers accompanied by dependent offspring had higher HCC compared to solitary males and females (support prediction 1). We also found that both yearling and twoyear-old dependent offspring had higher cortisol levels compared to all other bear groups (support prediction 2) including females with dependent offspring. Dependent offspring had higher HCC compared to all other social categories, and yearling brown bears had higher HCC as two-year olds (support prediction 2).

The higher HCCs in mothers with dependent offspring are likely related to the high energetic demands for rearing offspring, mainly lactation (Farley & Robbins 1995;Lopéz-Alfaro et al. 2013;Mislan et al. 2016). During peak lactation in brown bears (when offspring are ~150-250 days old) offspring consume around 1200 grams milk per day or approximately 2800
Kcal/day (Farley & Robbins, 1995). This means that a mother of two is transferring over 5000

Kcal to her offspring each day, not including the energetic costs to produce milk. Within this study population, the average energy content of the "typical" bear diet is 3.24 Kcal (Mikkelsen et al., 2023), so a mother nursing two offspring would need to eat over 1.5 kg of food each day just to support lactation demands. Differences in diet, specifically greater carnivory, are sometimes associated with greater metabolic demands in male brown bears due to their larger body sizes (Jacoby et al., 1999;Welch et al., 1997), but our result indicate that there is little difference in cortisol concentrations between solitary males and females, and solitary males had the lowest cortisol concentrations. If cortisol is an accurate proxy for metabolic demands (Romero, 2002), males in our sample had the lowest metabolic demands, even after accounting for age (and incidentally accounting for body size). Thus, high concentrations of cortisol in lactating females likely reflects a combination of the diverse roles cortisol plays within the body.
The high HCCs recorded in dependent offspring and their mothers are in line with other studies in Ursids (Mislan et al. 2016;Cattet et al. 2018)

Our findings add important pieces of knowledge about the role that social status linked to age may have in shaping the physiological response in mammals, although this response is often species-specific (reviewed in Heimbürge et al. 2019). The higher cortisol concentrations observed in mothers with dependent offspring are likely linked to the high energetic demands required to rear offspring. In the same way, the higher cortisol levels recorded in offspring accompanying mothers might be associated with direct cortisol transfer during lactation, similar physiological response to environmental stressors, increasing costs linked to growth (supported by the declining trend in terms of HCCs we observed in individuals from one to two years old of age), reduced surface: volume ratio, and/or adaptation to the new environment. Furthermore, another aspect not evaluated in this research might be attributable to the presence of more siblings within the same litter, which might lead subordinate cubs to experience chronic stress due to the presence of more dominant individuals.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Much of evolutionary and life history theory is based on the concept of trade-offs between reproduction and longevity (Errington, 1956;Selye, 1938). Different allocations of limited dietary energy and protein between reproduction and general tissue maintenance, growth, and resource storage (somatic growth), has resulted in a continuum of life-history strategies.

Species which prioritize somatic growth have a slower pace of life relative to those that prioritize reproduction (Pianka, 1970;Ricklefs and Wikelski, 2002). Long-lived species tend to have slow-paced lives-maximizing somatic growth at the cost of current reproduction (Ricklefs and Wikelski, 2002).

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Within the slow-fast continuum, there is variation in phenotypes among populations and individuals (Van De Walle et al., 2023), as factors such as environmental stochasticity (Ferguson & McLoughlin, 2000;Wright et al., 2019) (Pianka, 1970;Ricklefs & Wikelski, 2002). This could manifest in phenotypes with greater number of offspring per reproductive attempt (Wallace et al., 2007) or greater offspring size, particularly offspring size relative to maternal size or body condition (Rollinson et al., 2016).

While larger females tend to have larger offspring in greater numbers (Rollinson & Rowe, 2016;Wallace et al., 2007), it is unclear whether larger females invest relatively more in their offspring. To capture how maternal investment varies with resource availability, a better metric may be maternal size relative to offspring, i.e., explaining the variation in the

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore difference between maternal and offspring mass. For example, resource-rich females may be able pay the cost of both producing large offspring and investing heavily in self-maintenance while a resource-poor female may sacrifice somatic growth to also produce large offspring.
The former scenario would result in a larger difference between maternal and offspring size than the latter scenario.

Estimates of diet quality, such as stable isotopes, are also important to understand maternal investments (He et al., 2016). Many natural systems are limited by fixed nitrogen (Denno & Fagan 2003), which makes it an important resource to track among individuals. Energy, fixed nitrogen, and 15 N density all increase at higher trophic levels (Hobson et al. 1994, Layman & Post 2008), thus the ratio of heavy to standard nitrogen isotopes (δ 15 N; 15 N: 14 N) can be used as an indicator of relative diet quality, i.e., higher δ 15 N = higher density of energy and fixed nitrogen (Boecklen et al., 2011;Hobson et al., 1994). Therefore, mothers with higher δ 15 N values should have a better-quality diet and have more resources to invest in reproduction (Grindstaff et al., 2005).

Diet and resource availability are important factors in both reproduction and growth, and poor diet quality or greater competition for resources often results in smaller individual body sizes or decreased reproduction, as individuals struggle to obtain enough resources to meet their physiological demands (Grindstaff et al., 2005). In long-lived species, if resources are limited, we expect maternal investment in reproduction to decrease, resulting in smaller litters or smaller offspring sizes rather than smaller body sizes (Pianka, 1970). Here, we examine patterns in physiological indicators of body condition and diet to estimate maternal investment and describe the extent to which a species with a classic "slow pace of life" will sacrifice somatic growth to fuel reproduction. We use a population of brown bears (Ursus arctos) in Sweden (1995 -2019) with relatively small-bodied females but high reproductive output as a model to test whether 1) females in this population invest more in current

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore reproduction than somatic growth, and 2) whether reproductive investment changes with physiological condition and resource demands (i.e., litter size and bear density). We used a body condition index and δ 15 N values of females to represent maternal stored energy and diet quality. We used these same metrics in her offspring to estimate maternal investments through the transfer of mass (i.e., all resources used to build tissues) and δ 15 N from mothers to their offspring. We expect 1a) mothers will invest more in their own somatic growth than current reproduction and 1b) positive relationships between mothers and offspring for both body condition (Dahle et al., 2006) and δ 15 N values (Jenkins et al., 2001). Additionally, we expect that 2a) the difference in mass and δ 15 N values between mothers and offspring will depend on maternal age, body condition, and diet; as well as when there are fewer resource demands (i.e., litter size and conspecific density).

div.head: Study System
div.p: We used data on females with yearling offspring from a wild population of individually marked brown bears in Gävleborg and Dalarna counties in southcentral Sweden between (for full study area description, see Zedrosser et al., 2006). The brown bear population in Scandinavia was estimated in 2008 at ~3300 individuals and again in 2018 at ~2750 individuals in 2018; density varies but can reach 3 bears per 100 km 2 in the study area (Bischof et al., 2020;Kindberg et al., 2011). Their population remained relatively stable between 2004 and 2012 (Kindberg & Swenson, 2018), showing a slight increase from 2012 to 2015 (Bischof et al., 2020). Brown bears are born in January/February, spend their first months nursing in the den, and the rest of the year nursing and foraging with their mother before denning together for a second winter (Table 1).

div.head: Field Methods
div.p: Bears were captured in the spring (March through May) soon after den emergence via an immobilizing drug from a helicopter (Arnemo and Evans, 2017) Brown bears were born in January/February the year prior to capture and spent their first months nursing in the den, then spend the rest of the year nursing and foraging with their mother before denning together for a second winter, after which they were captured and sampled (Table 1). Brown bear hair grows ~ late April -October the year prior to sampling (Cattet et al., 2018;Jacoby et al., 1999). Thus, offspring hair samples were grown over a period in which they were still dependent on the mother but ingested a mixture of milk and solid foods. Hair is a mostly inert tissue, thus only represents the diet while it is grown (Kumar et al., 2012). Meanwhile, body mass is specific to the time it is measured. This means that there is a temporal mismatch between when diet indicators (δ 15 N) are stored in hair (spring through summer) and when we collected mass (the spring after hair is grown).

Diet during the active season is related to a bear's body condition at den entry (Swenson et al., 2007;Zedrosser et al., 2006) and their subsequent body condition at den emergence in the spring (López-Alfaro et al., 2013;Robbins et al., 2012). Thus, while there is a temporal mismatch between our δ 15 N values and mass, diet during the active season affects mass and body condition the following spring.

div.head: Lab Methods
div.p: δ 15 N values were measured from guard hairs that had large surface contaminants removed and were weighed to the nearest milligram. We followed the protocol in Macbeth et al. (2010) for cortisol concentration measurement and samples for stable isotope estimation were portioned out after the grinding step (Sergiel et al., 2017;Appendix S1). We used 40 μl HPLC grade methanol/ mg hair to wash away small surface contaminants. Each sample was washed three times for 3 min per wash (Sergiel et al., 2020), followed by at least 24 hours of air drying. We then ground samples to a fine powder in a mixer mill (Retsch MM4000; Retsch GmbH, Germany) at 30 Hz, and then put the powder into plastic vials. We followed Koehler et al. ( 2019) and weighed 1 mg of powdered hair into tin capsules and combusted encapsulated hair at 1030°C in a Carlo Erba NA1500 or Eurovector 3000 elemental analyser.

N2 from hair combustion was separated chromatographically and sent through an Elementar Isoprime or a Nu Instruments Horizon isotope ratio mass spectrometer. We used two reference materials to normalize the results: BWBIII keratin and PRCgel (δ 15 N = +14.31 and δ 15 N= +5.07 per mil, respectively). Within run (n = 5) precision was determined from both reference and sample duplicate analyses. QA/QC controls were ± 0.1 per mil. Isotope values are reported on the parts per thousand scale (‰) with the standard δ-notation (Tieszen et al., 1989).

div.head: Covariate development Predictors
div.p: Residual Maternal Mass. We fitted a linear regression model that predicted maternal mass (kg) using age and structural size (head circumference (cm); Dahle et al., 2006) as fixed effects, and year and individual ID as random effects (Appendix S2; Cattet et al., 2002;Rode The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore et al., 2020). We used individual residuals, i.e., the difference between the observed and predicted maternal mass as body condition index. Residual maternal mass represents resources a female has remaining in spring after reproduction and hibernation and should be considered relative to other females in the population.

Maternal δ 15 N values. We used δ 15 N values measured from female guard hairs as indicators of diet quality during the first active season after cub birth (Table 1). Females with higher δ 15 N have diets with a greater proportion on higher-trophic foods, which are considered higher quality.

Maternal age. Age of mothers the year offspring were born as determined from monitoring (i.e., many females were captured as yearlings with their mothers, thus individual age is known). When year of birth for a female was unknown from monitoring efforts (i.e., the female was captured the first time as an adult), we removed a pre-molar and determined age by counting the annuli (Harshyne et al., 1998).

Litter size. Number of known offspring a female produced in a specific year. Number of offspring was determined by visual counts of cubs of the year accompanying radio-collared females shortly after den emergence in April or May.

Annual mean bear density. We used an annual mean population density index (Frank et al. 2018) which was based on genetic data from feces to individually identified bears (Appendix S2) during 1998-2015. Years outside this range were predicted using the fitted quadratic relationship between year and annual mean bear density. To ensure that predicted bear densities did not result in erroneous relationships, we compared model results from our full dataset to a subset of the data that only included 1998-2015 (Appendix S2).

div.head: Response variables
div.p: Offspring mass. Offspring growth in all aspects (skeletal size, organ development and size, as well as fat deposits) are all indicators of the energy, matter, and nutrients females have transferred to offspring through gestation, lactation, and shared foraging (Gutierrez et al., 2012). Thus, we used mass (kg) to represent maternal investment in offspring, rather than standardize offspring mass by structural size (Wishart et al., 2024). Brown bear yearlings were measured at similar stages of development, thus differences in structural size are important to consider, as it either indicates cubs that were born earlier in the den (Friebe et al., 2013;Robbins et al., 2012) or which have grown faster.

Mass difference. To determine if the relationship between maternal and offspring mass varied with maternal physiology or diet, we used the difference between maternal and offspring mass during capture as a response variable.

Offspring δ 15 N values. Until offspring are independent of milk for nutrition, offspring tissues are at least partially built from resources derived directly from their mothers. Thus, offspring δ 15 N values partially represent their solid diet, as well as nutritional components from their mothers. A female investing more in her current reproductive effort may route more 15 N to milk production and less to body tissue maintenance (Miller et al., 2011) or break down body tissues (which are enriched in 15 N) to harvest nitrogen for milk production (Taillon et al., 2013).

δ 15 N ratio. We calculated the ratio of maternal δ 15 N values to individual offspring δ 15 N values, which should illustrate variation in the joint physiological processes that dictate maternal use of 15 N in milk production (Miller et al., 2011) and offspring assimilation of 15 N into tissues (Lübcker et al., 2020).

div.head: Statistical analysis & model selection
div.p: Prior to analysis, we assessed the correlation among predictors and determined that all predictors had a Pearson correlation coefficient <0.5, except for residual maternal mass and age. Because age was included in the calculations of residual maternal mass, these predictors were never included in the same model (Table 2). We used Bayesian linear regression models in JAGS and R (Plummer, 2003;R Core Team, 2023) to estimate the relationships between physiological indicators of maternal investment (offspring mass, mass difference, offspring δ 15 N values, and δ 15 N ratios) and predictors. Models were built based on a priori hypotheses and included additive effects as well as simple interactions (Appendix 1, Table S1). All models were run with a normal distribution, flat priors, litter ID, and maternal ID as random effects. Litter ID is a year-and litter-specific covariate that accounted for variation both among mothers and years. All continuous variables were standardized with a ztransformation prior to analysis. Models were run with four chains for 1,000,000 iterations with a burn-in of 100,000 iterations and a thinning rate of 20. We calculated a Bayesian pvalue for each model to evaluate the goodness of fit (Conn et al., 2018). Because it is well documented that maternal and offspring mass are highly correlated, maternal mass was automatically included in the model explaining variation in offspring mass and this was considered our "null" model. We did the same for offspring δ 15 N: the "null" model included the intercept and maternal δ 15 N. All additional models were compared to the null model to determine if additional fixed effects were sufficient to explain additional variation in the data.

We used a build-up modeling procedure, in which we first tested for non-linear relationships and retained the simplest relationship throughout model building (Table S1). Any covariates that had more support than the null model were used to build more complex models. We used an information-theoretic approach by comparing ΔDIC values among models and leave-one-out cross-validation to compare the strength of evidence among models (Burnham & Anderson, 2002;Gelman et al., 2013;Vehtari et al., 2017). When evaluating the strength

Mothers ranged in ages from 5-24 years (median 10), but most females were 8-13 years (first and third quantile, respectively).

For example, a female brown bear with a maternal residual mass of 1 (a female that weighs 1 kg more than expected given her age and skull circumference) has offspring with a predicted mass of 21.74 kg and a female with residual maternal mass of 2 has offspring predicted to be 21.95 kg. Each 1 kg increase in residual maternal mass is associated with a 0.21 kg increase in offspring mass. Meanwhile, a female with a residual maternal mass of 1 is predicted to be 68.27 kg heavier than her offspring. A female with residual maternal mass of 2 is predicted to be 69.03 kg heavier than her offspring, which means that for each 1 kg increase in residual maternal mass, females become 0.76 kg heavier than their offspring. Together, for each 1 kg increase in residual maternal mass, the difference between mother and offspring is growing ~3.5x faster than offspring mass is increasing (0.76/0.21 = 3.62).

When we used δ 15 N ratios as the response variable, the null model (intercept and maternal δ 15 N) had the most support (Table S1). Thus, there was no support for any of our hypothesized relationships regarding δ 15 N and maternal investments.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: Patterns in maternal investments indicated that mothers in this study population invest more in their own somatic growth than in current reproduction. The investment in each

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore reproductive bout depended on the mother's body condition, as well as competition for her resources, such as greater demand for milk with greater litter size and increasing competition for food with greater bear density. Even though our results agree with prevailing life-history theory (Ricklefs & Wikelski, 2002;Royauté et al., 2018;Wright et al., 2019), they do not explain the relatively small adult female body size and high reproductive output (Zedrosser et al., 2011) in this population.

Offspring mass increased with greater residual maternal mass (as has been seen in many different genera; Gutierrez- Marcos et al., 2012;Ronget et al., 2018), but the difference in mass between mothers and offspring increased ~3x faster than offspring mass (Figure 1 A & B). Offspring mass was also lower in years with greater bear density, which is expected due to increased competition for foods among conspecifics (Gaidet & Gaillard, 2008;Zedrosser et al., 2006). However, the difference in mass between mothers and their offspring was greater in years with higher bear densities (Figure 1 C & D). This indicates that females are conservative and selfish, and when competition for food increases, females pass the burden onto their offspring. Similarly, offspring mass was lower in larger litters, but the difference between mothers and their offspring was greater in larger litters (Figure 1 E & F), again hinting that as competition for resources increased (i.e., more offspring competing for milk), the resource burden is passed to offspring rather than born by the female (i.e., she won't necessarily produce more milk to produce larger offspring in a larger litter). Under these scenarios of increased competition, females were unable to either acquire or allocate more resources towards reproduction to maximize offspring size even though, theoretically, females should invest more resources in fewer offspring to increase offspring survival under greater population density (Sinervo et al., 2000). This is the epitome of a slow-pace of lifeprioritizing somatic growth over reproduction (Ricklefs & Wikelski, 2002;Wright et al., 2019).
Despite the comparatively small body size of adult females in this brown bear population, there is no indication that mothers must sacrifice somatic growth to maintain reproduction,

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore which would have been indicated by a negative slope between mass difference and residual maternal mass, bear density, or litter size.

Because maternal body size is associated with higher fitness within brown bears (Dahle et al., 2006;Hilderbrand et al., 2018) and across taxa (Dmitriew, 2011), ecologists may fall into the trap of assuming that bigger is always better, however individuals or populations that exhibit smaller body sizes may represent different, but equally fit phenotypes (Fergusson & McLoughlin, 2000;Zedrosser et al., 2011;Zamudio et al., 1995). Differences in body size and reproductive output among populations are typically attributed to threat of predation (Dmitriew, 2011) or landscape productivity and diet (Huston & Wolverton, 2011;Lester et al., 2007) -particularly carnivory and salmon consumption in brown bears (Hilderbrand et al., 1999;Mowat & Heard 2006). Even though bears in this population have diets low in meat and protein (Mikkelsen et al., 2023), there is no evidence that protein-and energy-rich foods are limited in this population (Frank et al., 2015;Jensen et al., 2020). Therefore, we propose alternative selection pressures that may explain the observed pace of life phenotype: an unpredictable environment and human persecution.

Stable environments are associated with dense populations of large individuals (Hilderbrand et al., 2018;Wright et al., 2019) while stochastic environments are associated with sparse, small, fecund individuals (Ferguson & McLoughlin, 2000;Wright et al., 2019). Thus, variation in population characteristics may be driven by resource and environmental predictability rather than overall landscape productivity, per se (Muniz et al., 2021). The extreme seasonality in Scandinavia, and the dependence on variable fruit production may favor relatively fast pace of life phenotypes compared to other brown bear populations.

Humans can also have strong effects on wildlife-inducing changes in behavior (Hertel et al., 2016;Ordiz et al., 2013) and allelic frequencies (Almeida-Rocha et al., 2020). In Europe, brown bears have a long history of human persecution (Zedrosser et al., 2011). Bear harvest in Sweden is mostly indiscriminate across adult age classes and sexes (Steyaert et al., 2016), resulting in relatively low adult survival (Van de Walle et al., 2021). When adult survival is low, selection should favor phenotypes that invest more in current reproduction (Kozłowski et al., 2020;Wright et al., 2019). Thus, centuries of human induced reduction in adult survival may have inadvertently favored smaller, more fecund phenotypes in this population.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Reproductive investment by female brown bears varied by maternal body condition and energetic demands. Females prioritized their own somatic growth over that of current reproduction, and when litter size or bear density increased, females seemed to pass the burden of greater competition for resources onto their offspring. Thus, we did not find evidence that females in the population must sacrifice growth to maintain reproduction, and resource limitation is not the cause of their relatively small sizes. Rather, local adaptations to the environment and human persecution may have led to a more-balanced allocation between somatic growth and reproductive effort relative to other brown bear populations, resulting in smaller body sizes and higher fecundity.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Body size is an important life history trait that affects both reproduction and survival (Stearns 1992, Robbins et al. 2012), and is a product of both natural selection (Stearns 1992, Andersson 1994) and human-caused selection (Coltman et al. 2003, Hutchings and Fraser 2008, Darimont et al. 2009, Zedrosser et al. 2011). Animals that are larger than average given their age have higher fitness: they have higher probabilities of survival, reproduce earlier in life, and have more and larger offspring (Stearns 1992, Robbins et al. 2012). Agespecific size is a function of competing resource demands and evolutionary pressures, creating a trade-off between growth rate and earlier reproduction (Stearns 1992). Quantifying

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore and understanding the similarities and differences in determinants of growth rate and maximum size between and within populations enables us to understand different ecological and evolutionary pressures, which results in better wildlife management (Rughetti andFesta-Bianchet 2011, Hamel et al. 2012).

One aspect of effective management is understanding the environmental and evolutionary mechanisms responsible for population dynamics. Population growth and stability can be partially or primarily driven by reproductive output and female survival (Saether et al., 2013), and there exists a natural trade-off in which organisms must split finite resources between their own growth and reproduction (Stearns, 1989). Both food availability and the severity of the environment affect the balance between resources available within the environment (Kim et al., 2017;Stoner et al., 2018) and the energetic cost to survive, grow, and reproduce (Romero et al., 2009). Thus, understanding the links between the environment, growth, and asymptotic body size provides important information for explaining current population growth rates as well as predicting future changes.
Changes in resource availability may disproportionally affect females because reproduction is generally costly (Stearns 1992),but particularly so for females (Lopez-Alfaro et al., 2013).

Females who cannot acquire enough energy may fail to reproduce (Lopez-Alfaro et al., 2013) or produce offspring with lower fitness (Hilderbrand et al., 2019). Variation in the number and size of offspring, as well as the time required for them to reach independence varies with maternal resource availability, often inferred through body size (Dahle et al., 2006;Hilderbrand et al., 2019;Robbins et al., 2012). Thus, body size is typically an honest representation of fitness and reproductive potential.
Body size can vary considerably across a mammal's distributional range (e.g. Herfindal et al. 2006, Szuma 2008, McDonough and Christ 2012). Comparing populations of the same

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore species in different parts of their range may reveal different landscape and evolutionary pressures that explains variation in body size (e.g., Festa-Bianchet and Apollonio 2003 and citations therein) and results in more effective management (Carey 2005).

The brown bear (Ursus arctos) is a large terrestrial mammal with a Holarctic distribution (Servheen et al. 1999). Within brown bears, as well as across taxa, litter and/or offspring size are positively related to adult female size (Hilderbrand et al. 1999, Dahle et al. 2006, Zedrosser et al. 2011), and reproductive success in both sexes of brown bears is positively related to adult size (Zedrosser et al. 2007, Zedrosser et al. 2013). Here we compare interpopulation differences in age-specific body mass and size as well as the patterns and determinants of mass and size of brown bears in Alberta, Canada, and Sweden. Even Because bears living on the same continent in similar ecological communities have similar life histories (McLoughlin et al. 2000), we hypothesized 1) that bears in similar ecological communities but different continents would also have similar life histories, expressed through similar sex-specific asymptotic body size. We further evaluated if 2) ecological and environmental factors have different effects on the relationship between body mass and age, and body length and age of male and female brown bears between continents/populations.

We tested the null hypotheses 2a) that there are no differences in the effects of population density on body size of both sexes in Alberta and Sweden; 2b) that there are no differences in the effects of primary production on body size of both sexes in Alberta and Sweden, and 2c) that the presence of dependent offspring has a more negative effect on female body size in Sweden than in Alberta.

div.head: MATERIALS AND METHODS
div.p: Study areas. -The Swedish study area covered ~21,000 km 2 of intensively managed boreal forest in a rolling landscape in south-central Sweden (61°N, 14°E), and mountainous national parks and adjacent forested land in the north (67°N, 18°E), ca 600 km apart (Zedrosser et al. 2006). The forest is dominated by Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) and Norway spruce (Picea abies). Elevations range from 200 to 2,000 m, and timberline is located at 600-750 m. The climate is continental with cold winters (January mean: -7°C in south, -13°C in north) and short, warm summers (July mean: 15°C in south, 13°C in north). Snow cover lasts from late October until May, the growing season is <130-180 days, and precipitation averages 500-1,000 mm annually (Zedrosser et al. 2006).

The study area in Alberta, Canada (from now on referred to as Alberta), covered 132,000 km 2 , mostly in and adjacent to the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, from the American -Canadian border (49°N, 113°W) to central Alberta (55°N, 118°W), a distance of 760 km.

Elevations range from 200 to 3,700 m, alpine meadows, rocky areas, and glaciers dominate the highest elevations, and coniferous, deciduous, and mixed forests dominate the mountains and foothills region. Lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta), spruces (Picea englemanii, P. glauca, P. mariana), and firs (Abies lasiocarpa, A. balsamea) are common conifers, and quaking aspen (Populus tremuloides) is the most common deciduous species (Downing and Pettapiece 2006). The continental climate has cold winters (January mean: -5°C in south, -15°C in north) and short, warm summers (July mean: 17°C in south, 15°C in north). Snow cover lasts from late October until early May, the growing season is <160-185 days, and average precipitation is 450-900 mm annually (Downing and Pettapiece 2006).
Bear populations in both study areas have similar diets. Protein consumption is highest in spring and early summer, consisting of ungulate neonates in Alberta (Munro et al. 2006), and

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore ungulate neonates and insects (mainly ants (Formica spp., Camponotus spp.) in Sweden (Dahle et al. 1998). Summer and fall diets are dominated by graminoids, herbs, and berries (mainly buffaloberry (Shepherdia canadensis) and mountain huckleberry (Vaccinium membranaceum)) in Alberta, and mainly berries (especially bilberry (V. myrtillus), crowberry (Empetrum spp.), and lingonberry (V. vitis-idaea)) in Sweden (Munro et al. 2006, Stenset et al. 2016). Both populations are interior and do not have access to spawning salmon.
Brown bears in Alberta face interspecific competition with sympatric black bears (Ursus americanus) (Mattson et al. 2005, Sawaya et al. 2012). The brown bear is the only bear species in Europe.

Brown bears face resource extraction, agriculture, urbanization, and recreational activities in both areas (Nielsen et al. 2004, Nellemann et al. 2007). In Sweden, however, brown bears have increased from ~130 animals in the 1930s to >3,300 animals in 2008 (Kindberg et al. 2011), and have been hunted since the 1940s (Swenson et al. 1994). In contrast, there are ~700 brown bears in Alberta and the trend is unknown, although demographic information suggests that some populations within the province may be declining Capture and handling are described in Cattet et al. div.head: Calculation of individual population density index.
div.p: -In Sweden we estimated a population density index within 17.84 km (~1000 km 2 ) of an individual based on the methods of Zedrosser et al. (2006). We chose this radius/area because it approximates the median home range size of adult males in both Alberta and Sweden (Table 1), and because the effect of neighbouring females on each other's probability to reproduce disappears beyond 20 km between the females' home range centroids (Ordiz et al. 2008). In the southern portion of the Swedish study area, the population size was estimated based on a DNA analysis of scats in 2001 and 2002. The temporally corrected individual density index for

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore radio-collared individuals was based on the location of individual bears genetically identified by scat sampling (71% of the radio-collared bears were represented in the scat samples) and the population growth rate (Zedrosser et al. 2006). No corresponding population estimate was available for the northern portion of the study area, but virtually every adult male and female, and all subadult female bears were radio collared. We used the locations of radiocollared bears, corrected to include subadult males, and growth rate of the population to calculate an individual density index as in the south (Zedrosser et al. 2006).

To estimate an individual population density index in Alberta, we followed an approach similar to that in southern Sweden with one exception; we used results from population inventories for 5 of 7 population units in Alberta, based on DNA analyses of barbwiresnagged hair collected from 2004-2008 (Boulanger et al. 2009).

div.head: Calculation of Normalized Differential Vegetation Index (NDVI).
div.p: -The NDVI consistently correlates with vegetation biomass and dynamics in various ecosystems, and we used NDVI in the growing season as a predictor of habitat quality and productivity (Pettorelli et al. 2005b). Primary productivity is important for reproductive success in other species (Pettorelli et al. 2006), thus we expected it to be positively correlated with brown bear growth. NDVI tiles for Sweden were downloaded from http://glcf.umiacs.umd.edu/data/gimms/ (accessed September 2010). We calculated an integrated NDVI within a radius of 17.84 km (this radius approximates an area of 1000 km 2 ) around the center location of each individual for the months May-July (the capture and growing season) in the year of capture with Erdas Imagine software (Leica Geosystems 2010). The averaged NDVI grids were imported into ArcGIS 9.3.1 (ESRI). "NoData" was assigned to all open water bodies. We then smoothed the averaged layer with a moving window approach to calculate the mean NDVI for each pixel for each year within a radius of 17.84 km around a given pixel. We downloaded NDVI tiles for Alberta from http://glcf.umiacs.umd.edu/data/gimms/ (accessed October 2010) and calculated

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore a pixel-by-pixel mean for each grid of the months May-July 1999-2006 using ArcGIS 9.2 (ESRI) Spatial Analyst Raster Calculator. For each individual bear we calculated a mean home range center for May-July for each year. These home range centers were buffered by a radius of 10,000 m using Arc View 3.2 Zonal Statistics tool, and every buffer was then matched to the mean summer NVDI grid for that year.

div.p: Female age distribution was not significantly different between the study areas in either the mass data set (mean age Alberta: 7.6 ± 4.7 years, N = 70; Sweden: 7.0 ± 4.8 years, N = 397; two-sample t-test: t = 1.014, p = 0.314) or the length data set (mean age Alberta: 7.6 ± 4.7 years, N = 59; Sweden: 7.0 ± 4.8 years, N = 388; two-sample t-test: t = 0.837, p = 0.406;

Figure 3A-B). Male age distribution differed significantly between the study areas for both the mass data set (mean age Alberta: 8.0±4.8 years, Sweden: 6.2±4.5 years; two-sample t-test: t = 2.668, p = 0.009) and the length data set (mean age Alberta: 8.4±5.0 years, Sweden: 6.2±4.5 years; two-sample t-test: t = 3.089, p = 0.003). Due to the multiyear growth pattern of bears (Schwartz et al. 2003), to avoid age differences affecting the results, and to fulfill model assumptions of homogeneity, we truncated the larger Swedish data sets to obtain data sets with similar male age distribution by randomly selecting the same number of bears per age class as in the Alberta data set (Figure 2D-E). The CV of mass and length were 37.1% and 10.0%, respectively, in Alberta, and 37.8% and 8.7%, respectively, in the truncated data set in Sweden. In general, body mass increased nonlinearly with age following the von Beryalanffy growth curve in all models evaluating the determinants of male and female body size in Alberta and Sweden (Figures 3A-D, Figure 4A-E). The coefficients of variation (CV) of mass and length in Alberta were 19.8% and 6.4%, respectively, and 27.3% and 9.2%, respectively, in Sweden.

Variation in female mass between the study areas was best described by the habitat/reproduction model (AICcw = 0.76; Table 4, Figure 4A), which explained 68% (R 2 ) of the variation in female mass. Alberta females were heavier at ages ≥90% asymptotic mass (95% confidence interval and sample size, Alberta: 97.8-107.4 kg, n = 85 vs. Sweden: 90.9-94.4 kg, n = 199) and longer at ages ≥90% asymptotic length (Alberta: 168-172 cm, n = 99 vs. Sweden: 161-164 cm, n = 333). The area term and its interactions explained the most variation, followed by NDVI and its interactions, population density and associated interactions, and finally presence of cubs and associated interactions (Table 5A). Females in Sweden weighed less than in Alberta (Table 5A) and the positive effect of NDVI was smaller in Sweden than in Alberta. The most parsimonious model also contained effects of population density and its interaction with study area, as well as the interaction between absence/presence of dependent offspring and study area, however, the CIs of these variables and interactions contained zero (Table 5A).

Two models comparing the determinants of female length between Alberta and Sweden were within ∆AICc <2 (Table 4, Table 5B, Figure 4B-C). The most parsimonious model was the habitat model (AICcw = 0.52), which explained 53% of the variation in female length. The habitat/reproduction model was the second-most parsimonious model (∆AICc = 0.39; AICcw = 0.42) and explained 54% of the variation in female length. Females were smaller in Sweden. The averaged model also contained effects of NDVI and its interaction with area, population density and its interaction with area, as well as the absence/presence of dependent offspring and its interaction with study area, however, the CIs of all of these parameters and interactions contained zero (Table 5B).

The capture model was the most parsimonious model (AICcw = 0.63, Figure 4D) to explain variation in male mass between the study areas (Table 4) and explained 69% of the variation in male mass. The predicted mass-and length-at-age curves for male bears were almost
