Alberta males and Sweden males were similar in mass at ages ≥90% asymptotic mass (95% confidence interval and sample size, Alberta: 180.0-216.7 kg, n = 37 vs. Sweden: 186.0-203.5 kg, n = 63) and length at ages ≥ 90% asymptotic length n = 187). Confidence intervals for mass and length in Alberta males were larger than Swedish males, likely due to the smaller sample size of Alberta males. The coefficients of variation of male mass and length were similar in data sets reduced to contain the same number of individuals from both study areas.

Males captured later in the year were heavier (Table 6) and the interaction 'area*Julian day of capture' suggests that males in Sweden may have been lighter due to earlier capture dates, however the CI contained 0. Males in Sweden were captured on average on Julian day 122 ± 20 days (May 2 in nonleap years), whereas males in Alberta were captured on average on Julian day 139 ± 16 days (May 19 in nonleap years); the difference in capture dates was significant when evaluated with a two-sample t-test (t = 4.371, p < 0.001). The second-best model that explained variation in male mass was the habitat model (ΔAICc = 2.16).

The age model was the most parsimonious model to explain male body length (AICcw = 0.89; Table 4, Figure 4E) and explained 89% of the variation in length. The age model was our null model and contained only the nonlinear effect of age. The second-best model was the capture model (ΔAICc = 4.36), but all covariates in that model had CI's that contained zero.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: We found no differences between the study areas in mass and length for males but, did find differences in females (hypothesis 1a)-Swedish females were smaller than Alberta females and also reached primiparity earlier and at a smaller mass and length than females in

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Alberta. Population density had no effect on body size in males in either area (hypothesis 2a). However, we found weak support for an effect of density on female mass and length that differed between Alberta and Sweden. We did not find study area effects of NDVI on mass and length (hypothesis 2b) for males, but female mass was positively associated with NDVI, and the effect was stronger in Alberta females. There was weak support for the same pattern in female length. Within females, there was a negative effect of offspring presence on mass, which was stronger in the Alberta females than those in Sweden. There was only weak support for an effect of offspring presence and area on length.

Similar environments and selection pressures across continents has resulted in similar body sizes in male brown bears. Male reproductive success in polygynous, sexually dimorphic species is dependent on body size (Andersson 1994), and males probably have been selected to maximize growth rate (Clutton-Brock 1988). Similar environmental conditions should result in similar energetic demands and availability, which will also lead to similar life history traits (Ferguson and McLoughlin 2000). Males in Alberta and Sweden both reached 90% asymptotic size and length at the same age (Fig. 1, Table 2), suggesting similar environmental conditions and energy availability between the study areas.

Females reach 90% of their asymptotic size later in life and may trade growth for reproduction (Clutton-Brock et al. 1988, Festa-Bianchet et al. 1994), but the affect varies between areas. Female brown bears in both study areas attained 90% asymptotic length and mass at similar ages (Figure 1, Table 2). However, Alberta females were 5% larger (8 cm) and 9% heavier (8 kg) at 90% asymptotic length and mass than females in Sweden. In mammals, female sexual maturity depends on reaching a threshold body mass, after which energy is allocated primarily to reproduction; age at primiparity in ungulates corresponds to the age when females reach ~80% of their adult mass (Gaillard et al. 2000). In general, bears seem to reach primiparity when relatively larger than ungulates, because females

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore reached primiparity at 93% and 84% of asymptotic mass in Alberta and Sweden, respectively. A trade-off between growth, reproduction, and hibernation may be responsible for this relatively larger threshold in bears. Brown bears may also keep their offspring for up to 5 years (Nawaz et al. 2008), which involves higher costs of lactation and maternal care, compared to ungulates, which usually wean their offspring at age 1. Female fecundity is strongly influenced by body mass in both ungulates (e.g. Garel et al. 2005) and bears (Hilderbrand et al. 1999, Zedrosser et al. 2011), with larger individuals generally reproducing earlier and producing more offspring of better quality (Clutton-Brock et al. 1988, Stearns 1992, Derocher and Stirling 1998b, Robbins et al. 2012). Females in Sweden and Alberta are both in the group of interior bears (Ferguson and McLoughlin 2000), with similar growth rates, despite geographic and genetic separation. Nevertheless, our data showed that the smaller and lighter Swedish females reproduced earlier, and had larger litters than the larger and heavier Alberta females (Fig. 1, Table 1) and other North American interior brown bear populations (McLoughlin et al. 2000, Zedrosser et al. 2011, Steyaert et al. 2012). It is a general pattern that female European brown bears produce larger litters in relation to body mass than females in North America (Zedrosser et al. 2011).

The continental differences we found in female reproductive investment may be caused by differences in persecution history (Zedrosser et al. 2011). Europeans conducted extermination campaigns for centuries with primitive weapons and traps; thus the mortality was likely nonselective and populations declined relatively slowly until effective firearms became available in the 1800s (Curry-Lindahl 1972, Swenson et al. 2000, Zedrosser et al. 2011). In much of northern North America, settlers arrived later and in smaller numbers, and brown bear populations have remained large over vast areas (Servheen et al. 1999). There is evidence of human-induced selection on morphology (Hendry et al. 2008) and life-history traits (Darimont et al. 2009) of wild animal populations, the latter especially from commercially exploited fish populations (Hutchings and Fraser 2008). Random harvest also

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore alters female reproductive strategies, with higher harvest rates causing lower body mass at primiparity (Proaktor et al. 2007). Thus, differences in long-term human selection pressure may have resulted in different reproductive strategies: earlier and higher reproductive investment in Swedish than Alberta bears (Zedrosser et al. 2011).

In addition to persecution history, indices of environmental conditions (such as NDVI) link primary productivity to animal performance (Pettorelli et al. 2005a) and female mass and length (e.g. Martinez-Jauregui et al. 2009). Correlations between plant phenology and carnivore life history traits likely operate indirectly through prey abundance (Melis et al. 2010); however, brown bears are omnivorous, not obligate carnivores and therefore may be more sensitive to primary productivity than other carnivores. We used NDVI values during the growing season to reflect plant growth and fruit production, and thus food availability and quality, because available nutrition is probably the most important factor affecting growth (Laws 1956). In contrast to other large mammals, bears partition their physical resources into growth and fat accumulation for hibernation. Bears depend upon various plants, especially berries, for fat accumulation in both Alberta and Sweden (Dahle et al. 1998, Munro et al. 2006). Although there may be no general a priori reason to expect conspecific populations in different areas to respond similarly to climate, as limiting factors may operate at different times of the year and the forms of regulation may differ (Martinez-Jauregui et al. 2009), bear populations in our study lived in areas with comparable ecological characteristics, which has been suggested to cause similar life history responses in brown bears (Ferguson andMcLoughlin 2000, McLoughlin et al. 2000). Nevertheless, the strength of the relationship between NDVI and body mass differed between areas. Swedish females weighed less with increasing NDVI than Alberta females, perhaps due to longer hibernation in Sweden (Table 1), or alternatively, because bears in Sweden were closer to carrying capacity. The earlier and higher reproductive investment of Swedish bears may be related to the different

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore population status of bears in the study populations (see above), or nutritional landscape characteristics that differed between areas.

Density-dependent relationships for body size and body mass have been reported in large mammals, especially ungulates (e.g., Clutton-Brock and Pemberton 2004), but also bears (Zedrosser et al. 2006). The effects of density and its interactions with study area were retained in the most parsimonious models explaining female mass and length, albeit never informative. Investigations on a more local/intra-population scale may reveal more pronounced effects of density on female life history traits, as has been suggested for Sweden (Zedrosser et al. 2006).

Life history theory predicts a trade-off between mass and reproduction when resources are limited (Stearns 1992), and reproduction and maternal care are costly for females (e.g. Pelabon et al. 1995). Female brown bears with dependent offspring weighed less than lone females in both areas, a pattern that has been found in several other mammals (e.g. Sand 1998, Pomeroy et al. 1999). Noninformative interactions between the absence/presence of dependent offspring and study area suggested area differences in the costs of reproduction.
More data, especially from Alberta, may be needed to better understand these differences.

The only informative variable explaining the differences in the determinants of mass and length of male bears in Alberta and Sweden was the positive effect of Julian day of capture on body mass. Males in Alberta were captured later in the year on average than in Sweden, which, together with a shorter denning period (Table 1), may be sufficient to explain differences in mass. Swenson et al. (2007) investigated the differences on body mass between brown bear populations in northern and southern Europe, and found that northern bears gained and southern bears lost mass during the spring, perhaps due to the greater availability and use of protein-rich food in spring in the north. Our results suggest that male

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore bears in Alberta also follow the northern European pattern of a relatively rapid increase in body mass after hibernation. Mattson et al. (2005) suggested that black bears could affect brown bears through reduced reproduction and recruitment caused by exploitation competition. Interspecific competition by American black bears therefore could affect brown bear life history in North America, potentially by causing smaller litter sizes and larger female body sizes in brown bears.

However, we found no evidence of such an effect in our results. Also, an analysis of the presence/absence effect of black bears on mean litter size in relation to mean adult female body mass in 19 brown bear populations suggested no such effect (Zedrosser et al. 2011).
Black bears are not present in Europe.

Many bear biologists and managers considered it a "commonly known fact" that brown bears are larger in North America than in Europe. However, our results suggest that, in comparable habitats and at the densities present in this study, at least males reach similar sizes.

Although habitat and population density also affect female size and mass, the larger variation in female growth and size may be related to differences in female reproductive investment (see also Hilderbrand et al. 1999, Zedrosser et al. 2011), due to differences in population trends, i.e., earlier reproduction in increasing populations or populations below carrying capacity, or to different selection pressures in the past, potentially due to human persecution (Zedrosser et al. 2011). Swedish brown bears exhibited characteristics typical of increasing populations, whereas Alberta bears exhibited characteristics typical of stable or decreasing populations. How fast such a switch in life-history strategies can occur in a large mammal with slow reproduction is unknown; however, it likely takes several generations (Zedrosser et al. 2011). For the manager and conservationist, the difference in reproduction investment means that bears in Sweden can be harvested at higher rates (Bischof and Swenson 2009, The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Bischof et al. 2009), whereas in Alberta bears must be managed more conservatively and stronger protective measures are needed to promote population increase.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The effects of climate change and plant phenological changes on herbivorous species are widely recognized (Plos et al., 2024), yet many omnivorous or carnivorous species also have some vegetative component to their diet (Thompson et al., 2007). The impacts of environmental variation in primary productivity on these species receives much less attention, despite potential ripple effects across the ecological community (Bartley et al., 2019;Gutgesell et al., 2022). For carnivores, particularly those termed "apex predators", prey availability is typically the primary focus for understanding diet and population dynamics (Gervasi et al., 2021;Hatton et al., 2015;Jonzén et al., 2013). The importance of apex predators to primary productivity, mostly through trophic cascades, has long been recognized (Schmitz et al., 2000), yet the reverse relationship is less-often explored (but see Hertel et al., 2018).

The term "carnivore" can be confusing in ecology, either referring specifically to members of the mammalian order carnivora, which is large and diverse, or more generally referring to mammals that kill and consume other vertebrates (i.e., meat-eaters; Yoshimura et al., 2021). These terms can be misleading because, outside a few families that are obligate carnivores (felids and hyenids; Clauss et al., 2010;Yoshimura et al., 2021), members of the order carnivora eat a wide variety of foods, including invertebrates, plants, or fungi (Edwards et al., 2011;Kauhala & Ihalainen, 2014;Kohl et al., 2015). Additionally, many species outside the order carnivora kill and consume vertebrates (i.e., other mammals such as primates and rodents, predatory birds, reptiles, amphibians, fishes, invertebrates, and plants (Caut et al., 2009;Cortes et al., 2014;Ellison & Gotelli, 2001;Valdez, 2020). Even though the order carnivora only accounts for ~10% of extant mammalian genera, the diversity within this group is extensive among all aspects of life -body size, reproductive output, home range size, social behavior, and diet (Carbone et al., 1999;Gittleman, 2013). The historical focus on simple interactions between large, charismatic,

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore obligate carnivores (typically an apex predator), and their large prey over-simplifies the roles of carnivores within ecological communities (Miller et al., 2001). This bias likely overlooks numerous trophic interactions which may be important to community stability (Cruz-Mcdonnell & Wolf, 2016;Garay et al., 2012;Hunter, 2009;Kohl et al., 2015;Kratina et al., 2012). This is particularly important given anthropogenic alterations to the environment.

Human modifications to the landscape, such as the conversion of wildlands to agriculture or timber production changes the structure of ecological communities and can interact with climate change to exacerbate changes in primary productivity (McRae et al., 2008;Pirotta et al., 2022).

For instance, timber harvest removes the physical protection and thermal buffering the overstory provides to understory plants (Santos et al., 2024), which makes them more vulnerable to extreme weather (Gallinat et al., 2015). Additionally, conversion of natural ecosystems into agriculture is associated with lower species diversity (Krebs et al., 1999;Tilman et al., 2001), which may be less resilient to perturbations (Landi et al., 2018), such as extreme weather events. Under most climate change predictions, extreme weather is going to become more frequent, which will likely affect primary productivity, community interactions, and increase annual variation (Cianfrani et al., 2018;Lane et al., 2012;Zang et al., 2017).

Changes in primary productivity will directly affect species that consume plants in addition to animal-derived foods (Hertel et al., 2018). Recent work has highlighted the important roles polyphagous species play within ecological communities, such as connecting, and stabilizing communities (Bartley et al., 2019;Gutgesell et al., 2022;Kratina et al., 2012). For instance, classic food webs with omnivorous species model them as static consumers exerting constant pressure on multiple resources (Gutgesell et al., 2022). However, polyphagous species can rapidly respond to changes in resource availability (Deacy et al., 2018), relieving pressure from an exhausted resource and while increasing pressure on another, more abundant resource, even if the second resource is a less-preferred food (Zhang et al., 2021). Thus, polyphagous species are predicted to have interactions with more species in their community, but each connection is weaker, creating redundancies within the community that have a stabilizing effect. Shifts in primary productivity that alter polyphagous species' foraging patterns, even apex predators, may result in community rewiring (Gutgesell et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2021).

Because diet and predation pressure can have strong effects on growth and reproduction (Relyea & Auld, 2005;Ronget et al., 2018), changes in ecosystem structure will likely manifest in life-history changes across community members (Massol et al., 2017). Despite the need for a deeper understanding of carnivore ecology beyond their roles as predators, correctly identifying and modeling environmental features to quantify alternative relationships is a challenge, due to the complex nature of ecological communities. Even within the same population of a single species, there will be differences in diet among demographic classes (Beck et al., 2007;Moorhouse-Gann et al., 2020), space-use strategies (Stern et al., 2024) and individual specializations (Edwards et al., 2011;Woo et al., 2008), which can obscure general patterns.

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Climate and plant life history synchronization (Pantis et al., 1994) results in landscape-wide synchronizations between primary productivity and consumer diet (Despland, 2018), making individual components difficult to separate. Changes in climate, weather, plant phenology, and consumer diets may also be subtle, requiring many years of data to detect patterns (Selås, 2000). Thus, another limitation to understanding the complex and subtle ecological relationships between carnivores and primary productivity is a lack of long-term data. Many researchers have tried to predict how species will respond to climate change by identifying important diet components and ecosystem characteristics limiting food availability. However, these studies are often data-limited and context specific. For example, bear species in North America and Japan change their movement in years of mast crop failures (Bogdziewicz et al., 2016;Kozakai et al., 2013;Schwartz et al., 2010) but the same patterns are absent in Sweden (Hertel et al., 2019).

We used stable isotopes measured in hair to estimate diet proportions and explain long-term patterns in diet and stable isotope values in a highly adaptable polyphagous carnivore, the brown bear (Ursus arctos). We used 25 years of data on known individuals in south-central Sweden and focused on the five primary diet components of bears in this system: ants (Formica spp. and Camponotus spp.), bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus), crowberry (Empetrum nigrum), lingonberry (Vaccinium vitus-vitae), and moose (Alces alces; Dahle et al., 1998;Stenset et al., 2016). Based on previous stable isotope diet analysis (Mikkelsen et al., 2023), we expected bilberry to make up the greatest proportion of the brown bear diet, however meat is a higher quality food than berries and meat is positively associated with fitness in brown bears (Hilderbrand et al., 1996). Thus, we expect brown bear diet to be driven by moose availability (Hypothesis 1). Specifically, we expect years with greater numbers of moose to be associated with greater proportions of moose in the diet. Moose populations have been increasing across Scandinavia (Jensen et al., 2020). Thus, we expect brown bears will capitalize on this increasing resource and proportions of moose in the diet should increase through time (Hypothesis 2). Annual variation in food productivity will also result in annual variation in stable isotope values (Hypothesis 3). Specifically, we expect δ 15 N values to be related to indices of moose population size and reproduction and δ 13 C values to be related to annual bilberry production.

div.head: Study system
div.p: Our study area encompassed ~13,000 km 2 in Gävleborg and Dalarna counties in southcentral Sweden with low human density and heavily managed forests of Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) and Norway spruce (Picea abies). Bears were captured by darting with an immobilizing drug from a helicopter (Arnemo & Evans, 2017) in spring soon after den emergence (March through 114

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore May). All capture procedures were conducted in accordance with the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency, Swedish Board of Agriculture, and Swedish Ethical Committee on Animal Research .

div.head: Stable isotope data
div.p: Brown bear hair samples were collected from between the shoulders of brown bears during spring captures . After collection, hair samples were placed in individual paper envelopes and stored dry at room temperature until they were processed for stable isotope measurement.

When processing brown bear hair, we separated underfur out of the sample, removed large surface contaminants, and weighed hairs to the nearest milligram. Preparatory procedures followed the protocol for cortisol concentration measurement (Macbeth et al., 2010) and samples for stable isotope estimation were portioned out after the grinding step (Sergiel et al., 2017;Appendix S2). We washed each sample three times with 40 μl HPLC grade methanol per mg hair for three minutes per wash to remove other external contaminants (Sergiel et al., 2020).

After the hair had dried for at least 24 hours, it was ground to a fine powder in a mixer mill (Retsch MM4000; Retsch GmbH, Germany) at 30 Hz and then put into plastic vials. To measure δ 13 C and δ 15 N in hair, we followed Koehler at al. (2019) and weighed 1 mg of powdered (treated) hair into precombusted tin capsules. Encapsulated hair was combusted at 1030°C in a Carlo Erba NA1500 or Eurovector 3000 elemental analyser. The resulting N2 and CO2 were separated chromatographically and introduced to an Elementar Isoprime or a Nu Instruments Horizon isotope ratio mass spectrometer. We used two reference materials to normalize the results to VPDB and AIR: BWBIII keratin (δ 13 C = -20.18, δ 15 N = +14.31 per mil, respectively) and PRCgel (δ 13 C = -13.64, δ 15 N= +5.07 per mil, respectively). Within run (n = 5) precisions as determined from both reference and sample duplicate analyses and from QA/QC controls were ± 0.1 per mil for both δ 13 C and δ 15 N. We corrected δ 13 C values for the anthropogenic depletion of 13 C in the atmosphere (i.e., the Suess Effect) by applying a -0.022‰ correction per year (Chamberlain et al., 2005) and used results from controlled feeding experiments on ursids (Felicetti et al., 2003;Hilderbrand et al., 1996;Rode et al., 2016) to estimate the isotopic discrimination factors (TDFs) between bear hair and bear serum (Appendix S1.a). We used a similar procedure to estimate TDFs between moose hair (which we sampled) and moose meat and offal (which is the tissue that brown bears eat; Appendix S1.b).

div.head: Estimating bear dietary proportions
div.p: We expected brown bear diet to vary among the reproductive classes of independent bears in our population (Rauset et al., 2012;Steyaert et al., 2013;Swenson et al., 2007), thus we

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore included the effect of demographic classes in our modeling procedures. To explore how brown bear diet varied through time and in response to environmental variables, we used two separate analyses. First, we subset the data by reproductive category (solitary females, females with dependent offspring, and solitary males) and ran three separate diet estimation models using year and bearID as random effects. We also ran a model that included an age category for the solitary males. Beyond the age of 21, we only had two males (aged 26 and 29), so we removed those two records from the age analysis. We did not include a model with age for the female reproductive categories because we had no biological basis to expect female diet to change with age. We used previous stable isotope diet estimates for our population (Mikkelsen et al., 2023) to derive informative priors for our models. We removed 6 outliers that had particularly high δ 13 C values and fell outside the mixing polygon. We suspect these bears were eating human-derived foods, such as domesticated grains or processed grain products that contain corn, which have different isotopic signatures than wild plants (Javornik et al., 2021) and were not include in our mixing polygon (Appendix S2). Each model was run with three chains with 3000000 iterations, a burn-in of 1500000 and a thin rate of 500. We used graphical output as well as fit statistics to determine if each model had run for sufficient time to converge and to ensure proper chain mixing (Semmens et al., 2009;Stock et al., 2018). All analysis was completed in R (R Core Team, 2024) using package MixSIAR (Stock & Semmens, 2013).

div.head: Annual variability in food availability
div.p: Berries. We used berry inventory information from the Siljansfors Experimental Forest where berry production was assessed at 54 permanent sites between 2006 -2020. The number of ripe bilberries were counted between July and end of August and the number of ripe lingonberries were counted between end of August and mid-September. Following Hertel et al. 2018 we calculated an annual berry production index as the annual deviation of berry abundance from the 11-year average for each plot. We then created a model to predict berry production with year as a fixed effect and then predicted the annual deviation of berries produced. This was scaled between 0 and 1 with 0 denoting years of low berry production and 1 denoting years of high berry production (Table 1).

Moose. Moose harvest data was downloaded from Statistik älgdata (https://algdata-apps.lansstyrelsen.se/algdatäa-apps-stat; Singh et al., 2014) for the counties of Gävleborg and Dalarna. Data in this system is citizen-reported moose observations prior to and during the moose hunting season adjusted by observer effort/observation hours. Reporting harvested moose is required by law in Sweden (Singh et al., 2014). The moose observations database also records the sex, age (calves and adults) and the number of calves with an observed female (singles vs twins), which indicates the overall moose population size, as well as the annual recruitment rate of calves surviving from birth in spring to the fall (Kalén et al., 2022). div.head: Linear regression modelling and model selection
div.p: We used mixed-effects linear regression models with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2014) in R (R Core Team, 2024) to explain variation in δ 13 C and δ 15 N values within our population based on a priori hypotheses that diet, and consequently stable isotope values would vary by sex, age, and annual resource availability (Table S1). We used individual ID and reproductive category as random effects and used a build-up modeling strategy in which we began by determining the best relationship for each covariate considered (linear, log-linear, or quadratic), and then retained that structure throughout modelling. All models were compared to the null model to determine whether fixed effects explained more variation than the intercept only, and variables that performed better than the intercept only were used to build more complex models that included additive effects and two-way interactions. We used an information-theoretic criterion for small sample sizes (AICc) and the relative differences between models (ΔAICc) when determining the model with the best fit given the data from which we derived final inferences (Burnham & Anderson, 2002). For models with similar AICc values, we compared beta estimates, the 95% confidence intervals around the beta estimates, and model variance to select the most parsimonious model (Anderson 2008).

Although we had bear data from 1995-2020, our annual food availability data was limited to 2006-2020, restricting our inference regarding the drivers of variation in δ 13 C and δ 15 N to this 14-year period. Prior to analysis, we compared the demographic composition, means, medians, and standard errors of our subset data to the full dataset to ensure there were no obvious differences in the data (Supplementary materials S3). Diet proportions were estimated for each demographic class separately, while we considered all demographic classes together for linear regression modelling.

div.head: RESULTS
div.p: After removing dependent offspring and bears with missing records for age or reproductive category, we had 669 records of 268 independent bears (aged 2-19) representing 1995-2020. The subset data in which we had annual bilberry production indices consisted of 410 records of 177 independent bears aged 2-19 representing 2006-2020.

div.head: General patterns of diet
div.p: The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore

Posterior diet estimates for all three reproductive categories indicated that bilberries made up the greatest proportion of the diet for males, females, and females with dependent offspring. Most posterior estimates agreed that crowberry made up a very small proportion of the diet, but the posterior distribution had a long righthand tail that largely overlapped with lingonberry estimates, indicating that we cannot be certain that lingonberry always makes up a larger proportion than crowberry (Figure S1). Despite their isotopic similarities (Figure S2), these two berry species had a low negative correlation (Figure S3), which strengthens our confidence in the posterior diet estimates and the model's ability to differentiate between these food sources. Higher-trophic, protein rich foods (moose and ants) made up small proportions of brown bear diets, but moose was highest in solitary adult males (~12.5%; Figure S1). Though moose and ants, like lingonberry and crowberry, are isotopically similar (Figure S2), the posterior distributions are unimodal and narrow, indicating good distinction between the two sources. Annual estimates of bilberry and lingonberry mirror one another (i.e., in years of high bilberry proportions in the diet, there are lower proportions of lingonberry; Figure 1 A-C). This is partially due to the mathematical constraints that proportions must sum to 1, so any reduction in one food source must result in an increase in others. However, this likely indicates consistent diet shifts between their preferred food, bilberry, and other food sources. When we consider only higher-trophic foods, ants and moose were consumed in similar proportions across years (Figure 1 D-E). Ants made up a consistently larger diet proportion in both female reproductive categories, while moose make up a larger proportion of the diet than ants in solitary males. There were two years in which we had no samples from solitary males (2014 & 2015).

When we looked at the diet composition throughout the study, there is evidence that the proportion of ants and moose have decreased, while the proportion of bilberry in the diet has remained stable or slightly increased (Figure 2).

div.p: There was annual variation in δ 15 N values that was consistent for all three demographic classes (Figure 4B). div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: We estimated long term trends in brown bear dietary composition from 25 years of δ 15 N and δ 13 C stable isotope data. Over the course of our study, the proportion of moose and ants in the bears' diet decreased while the proportion of bilberry increased, suggesting a shift away from clustered protein rich food sources towards dispersed carbohydrate rich food. These trends were functionally linked to interannual variation in bilberry abundance and moose calf recruitment: δ 15 N values increased with increasing bilberry productivity the year prior to hair growth, while δ 13 C values increased with bilberry productivity and moose calf recruitment.

Based on 25 years of stable isotopes measured in hair from known individual brown bears in south-central Sweden, brown bear diet was different between males and females, but there was little difference between the female reproductive classes (solitary females and females with dependent offspring). Bilberry made up the greatest proportion of the brown bear diet for all three demographic classes, but it was highest in adult males, and there was little difference between subadult males and the female reproductive categories. The proportion of higher trophic foods (moose and ants) was higher in males than females, and was highest in adult males, though there was still a lot of variation among adult males (Figure S1).

The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore Diet proportions were estimated based on stable isotope values of nitrogen and carbon, which had different annual variation, and the overall variation for each isotope was associated with different model covariates. δ 15 N values varied with bear age and bilberry production the year prior to hear growth. δ 15 N values increased with age for both sexes, but the affect was much stronger in males than females (Table 3; Figure 3). δ 15 N values also varied with bilberry productivity the year prior to hair growth, while δ 13 C values were best explained by bilberry and number of calves observed the same year hair was grown.

δ 13 C values were negatively correlated with both bilberry production and moose calf availability, yet these two foods are at opposite ends of the observed δ 13 C values in our system-bilberry has the lowest δ 13 C values, while moose have the highest. Thus, years with higher moose calf availability are associated with brown bear δ 13 C values that are less like moose values, indicating that moose made up a lower diet proportion in these years. Bears tend to predate moose calves in the spring soon after birth (Swenson et al., 2007). Moose calf observations are reported by the public in the late summer and fall (Statistik älgdata). Brown bears can be a substantial source of mortality for moose calves in Sweden (~25%; Swenson et al., 2007), therefore, the association of higher moose consumption in years of lower numbers of reported moose calves may be because bears have predated more moose calves in the spring, resulting in fewer calves to be counted in the fall. Prior to 2011, moose calf numbers fluctuated around 3000-4000 observed calves, then rapidly increased until numbers restabilized in 2014 around 13000 (Statistik älgdata). Yet, the proportion of moose in the diet does not increase with calf observations, which indicates that either moose calves are not a preferred food for bears, or calves have never been a limited food resource within this study population.

Among ants, moose, and bilberries, δ 15 N values measured in brown bear hair were most closely associated with the proportion of moose in brown bear diet. However, δ 15 N values were not associated with indices of annual moose availability, rather, they were best explained by an index of bilberry production. This indicates that while δ 15 N values are driven by the proportion of moose in the diet, diet itself is driven by primary productivity directly. Berries, particularly bilberries in our system, are extremely important for fat accumulation during hyperphagia (Dahle et al., 1998;Hertel et al., 2018;Stenset et al., 2016). Years of lower bilberry production may result in lower fat reserves prior to hibernation and, consequently, bears emerging in poorer condition in the spring (López-Alfaro et al., 2013;Robbins et al., 2012). Bears in poorer spring condition may have a stronger drive to replenish depleted energy stores and spend more time either scavenging moose carcasses or predating moose calves. Alternatively, indications of diet switching may be an artifact from the constraint that diet proportions must sum to 1. Bears may not change their behavior and modify their diet in years of poor bilberry production (Hertel et al., 2019). Instead, they may catabolize more of their own lean mass stores, which would also result in higher δ 15 N values (Lee et al., 2012) and artificially inflate the proportion of higher trophic foods. Catabolizing lean mass is typically associated with extreme starvation (Hobson et al.,120 The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore 1993), however in species adapted to long fasts with unique nitrogen cycling adaptations, lean mass may be more readily catabolized than in other species.

The population-wide, cyclic pattern of the δ 15 N values indicates large-scale processes, most likely related to climate and primary productivity. Further research is required to uncover the broader mechanisms driving these changes in brown bear diet and how diet shifts are related to brown bear population dynamics, such as reproduction, offspring survival, and recruitment (Keay et al., 2018). In the case of many carnivores, primary productivity is assumed to have an indirect effect, typically through prey responses to changes in primary productivity (Li et al., 2021;Stoner et al., 2018). However, berry productivity affects reproduction and body condition in our study system (Hertel et al., 2018) and our results indicate that diet is also driven by berry production, rather than moose availability.

These results add to the growing body of evidence that meat may be overemphasized in diets of polyphagous carnivores (Deacy et al., 2017;Erlenbach et al., 2014;Robbins et al., 2022;Rode et al., 2021), which may minimize the non-predatory roles these species play, such as nutrient cyclers and seed dispersers (Borchert & Tyler, 2011;Harrer & Levi, 2018;Reimchen, 2017;Steyaert et al., 2019;Takahashi et al., 2008). Beyond ursid species, modern monitoring tools, such as DNA metabarcoding and camera traps, and stable isotopes, have documented "novel" foraging behaviors in a wide variety of carnivores, such as sharks consuming seagrasses (Leigh et al., 2018), crocodilians consuming fruit and dispersing seeds (Platt et al., 2013), or wolves foraging on berries (Homkes et al., 2020). Including "a-typical" community interactions is imperative to fully understanding ecological function and resiliency

It is unclear how many other "top predators" are sensitive to changes in primary production, and hopefully future research on carnivorous species will widen its scope beyond predator-prey and producer-prey interactions. Given current projections of changes in phenology and species distributions due to climate change (Inouye et al., 2022), it is more important than ever to recognize the direct relationships between carnivorous species and both primary producers and prey species (Deacy et al., 2017). Ecological connections between weather and climate, primary productivity, and upwelling higher trophic effects are difficult to detect and untangle (Schmitz et al., 2000). For example, within Scandinavia, annual weather patterns explain little variation in annual berry production (Hertel et al., 2018;Selås 2000). This is because fruit production may be negatively affected by a short but extreme weather events or a complex interaction of conditions over the full growing season (Bokhorst et al., 2011;Orsenigo et al., 2014). Thus, it is difficult to understand how changes in climate will ultimately affect plant phenology and the many other species that rely on primary producers. Many carnivorous species may be doubly 121

div.p: Hairs used in this analysis were part of an on-going large-scale project that uses hair collected from bears for both cortisol and stable isotope analysis. div.head: Trophic discrimination factor calculations
div.p: When animals consume foods, isotopic values change between food source and consumer tissue by a (trophic) discrimination factor. Isotopic discrimination values vary by diet type, consumer tissue and species (Kurle et al., 2014), therefore, to derive reliable dietary estimates of diet using isotopic mixing models, appropriate trophic discrimination factors (TDFs) must first be estimated. We used linear models published from feeding experiments of several ursid species to estimate TDFs for each food source in our model (Felicetti et al., 2003;Hilderbrand et al., 1996;Rode et al., 2016). We then explored how variation in our TDFs (by allowing them to vary by 1.0) as well as applying published TDFs from other brown bear stable isotope research changed diet estimates in our model (Felicetti et al., 2003;Hilderbrand et al., 1996;Ro et al., 2021).

div.head: Moose hair to moose meat isotopic values
div.p: Because moose in our system were represented by hair samples, we first determined the TDF between moose diet and moose meat and hair. Feeding experiments are rare in wildlife species, particularly for large species. div.head: Effect of trophic discrimination factors on diet estimates
div.p: The effects of diet and metabolism on the life history of an omnivorous carnivore As expected, using different isotopic discrimination factors derived from the four different methods described above strongly affected diet estimates (Bond & Diamond 2011). TDFs calculated using our method and the equations from Hilderbrand et al. (1996) and Felicetti et al. (2003) were similar (Table S1) but resulted in very different diet estimates (Table S2). A small difference in the intercept (0.5‰) of the linear equation resulted in dietary proportions that varied by 0.02-0.22 (Table S2). When comparing diet estimates across the different TDFs, ants and moose had little variation in their estimates, while bilberries varied the most. Following methods in Ro et al., 2021 and using no TDFs, our consumers fell well outside the mixing polygon and the resulting estimates were highly skewed and unlikely (100% ant diet).

div.head: Differences between diet estimates using uninformative vs. informative priors
div.p: Uninformative priors (by definition) had a flat distribution, somewhat informative priors had mean proportions for each food source derived from previous scat analyses (Dahle et al., 1998;Persson et al., 2001;Stenset et al., 2016) with variation of 0.1%, while informative priors had the same means as the somewhat informative priors, but a much narrower distribution of 0.04% derived from standard deviations of the diet proportions from the scat analyses (Table S4).

When we used uninformative priors, the model converged on precise estimates of dietary proportions in our bear population (standard errors ranged from 0.03 to 0.14). When we used informative prior information from scat analysis, the model estimates were less precise. Using less-informative priors resulted in estimates very similar to those derived from uninformative priors, but with slightly larger standard errors (Table S4).

div.head: Bear density covariate
div.p: Following Frank et al. (2018) we used an annual mean population index to account for the growing bear population in Sweden 1995-2020. Individual bears were genetically identified using six microsatellites from collected bear faeces (Bellemain et al., 2005;Kindberg et al., 2011). Scat collection was not homogenous across counties and scat was not collected in all counties every year. They followed methods in Jerina et al. (2013) and used weighted values S2). div.head: Moose hair to moose meat isotopic values
div.p: Because moose in our system were represented by hair samples, we first determined the TDF between moose diet and moose meat and hair. Feeding experiments are rare in wildlife species, particularly for large species. We used published results of controlled feeding experiments on bison (Bison bison), elk (Cervus elaphus), caribou (Rangifer tarandus), and moose (Alces alces) to estimate the isotopic discrimination between ungulate hair and muscle under equilibrium conditions (Drucker et al., 2010;Milakovic & Parker, 2013;Rioux et al., 2020;Tieszen & Boutton, 1989). Values of δ 13 C between hair and blood or muscle ranged from 0.99‰ in elk to 1.01‰ in bison and δ 15 N ranged from 0.77‰ in elk to 1.0‰ in bison. div.head: ABSTRACT
div.p: The effects of climate change and plant phenology on herbivorous species are widely recognized, yet many carnivorous species also have vegetative components to their diet. Environmental variation in primary productivity on these species receives much less attention, despite potential ripple effects across the ecological community. We used 25 years of stable isotope data measured in hair to estimate diet proportions of five primary diet components and explain long-term patterns in diet in a highly adaptable polyphagous carnivore, the brown bear (Ursus arctos). We used a two-step approach in which we first used Bayesian mixing models to estimate annual dietary proportions, and then used linear regression models to explain the variation in diet components and stable isotope signatures. Based on previous stable isotope diet analysis, we expected soft mast to make up the greatest proportion of the brown bear diet, however meat is a higher quality food and is positively associated with fitness in brown bears. Thus, we expect brown bear diet to be driven by animal-derived foods (Hypothesis 1). Thus, we expect brown bears will capitalize on increasing moose (Alces alces) populations and proportions of moose in the diet should increase through time (Hypothesis 2). We also expect annual variation in food productivity will result in variation in stable isotope values (Hypothesis 3). We found that diet did not change with increasing moose availability and variation in both δ 13 C and δ 15 N were highly correlated with the bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) productivity index, indicating that diet in this "apex predator" is driven by primary productivity, rather than prey

div.head: Estimation of dietary macromolecules and energy
div.p: To estimate the percent dry proportion of the diet of the studied brown bear population that corresponded to macromolecular composition (e.g., proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids), we used the estimated dietary proportions from the simmr model and nutritional information from previous bear studies and the USDA National Nutrient Database (Coogan et al., 2014;Erlenbach et al., 2014;Swenson et al., 1999;USDA, 2018;Table S3) to estimate the dietary proportion of each macromolecule for each dietary endpoint in our model. We used the average percent dry matter of proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids for each food group (moose, ants, and berries; Table S3) and multiplied that by the proportion of the overall diet represented by each group (Table S4). The sum of the three groups provided an estimate of the proportion of the diet made up of each macronutrient, as well as each food group's macronutrient contribution to the diet (Coogan et al., 2014;Erlenbach et al., 2014). For example, our stable isotope models estimated that bear diet was approximately 4% moose, 7% ants, and 89% berries. div.head: S1. Laboratory methods (cortisol vs stable isotope procedures)
div.p: Hairs used in this analysis were part of an on-going large-scale project that uses hair collected from bears for both cortisol and stable isotope analysis. Originally, hair samples were prepared following typical stable isotope procedures as described in Hobson et al. (2000). After publishing lab experiments that showed that using standard preparatory procedures for cortisol extraction were also compatible for stable isotope extractions, a single preparatory procedure was adopted and used for both stable isotope and cortisol extraction (Sergiel et al., 2017). Therefore, some hairs in this analysis were prepared using different methods, but this should have very little effect on stable isotope extraction, results, or interpretations. Hair samples that were processed using the single preparatory procedures were prepared following Sergiel et al. div.p: When animals consume foods, isotopic values change between food source and consumer tissue by a (trophic) discrimination factor.
